harder.updated_question: Apps for diabetic foot ulcers Assessment and Monitoring
harder.verification_criterion: The answer lists at least one mobile application specifically designed for diabetic foot ulcer assessment and/or monitoring.

attempts.answer:
Below is a practical, evidence-backed overview of mobile apps and digital tools for assessing and monitoring diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs), organized by function and supported by clinical/technology studies.

Why digital tools matter for DFUs
- DFUs impose high healthcare use and risk; early detection, frequent monitoring, and timely escalation are key to avoiding amputation and hospitalization. <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">Telemedicine for DFUs was non‑inferior to usual care for healing within 12 months, reduced amputation, and showed no mortality difference</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">mobile tools can enhance self‑care, remote monitoring, and early complication detection</cite>. However, <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">variability in study designs and outcomes limits firm effect size comparisons</cite> and <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">more standardized, long‑term trials are needed</cite>.
- Digital workflows align with guideline recommendations: <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">IWGDF emphasizes patient education, regular foot examination, footwear care, and skin care, which map to mobile app features and telehealth triage</cite>.

Core categories of DFU apps and representative tools

1) Telemedicine and remote wound assessment platforms
- Function: Secure video consults, photo documentation, guided questionnaires, clinician triage, and care-plan tracking. They enable routine follow‑up, early detection of worsening, and reduced in‑person load. <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">Telemedicine reduced amputation risk and was non‑inferior for healing at 12 months vs usual care</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-4">a rural RCT found similar healing (32% vs 28%) and amputation rates (23% vs 25%) between nurse‑led telemedicine and usual care over 12 weeks</cite>. 
- Integration tips: Many platforms pair smartphone photos with structured grading. <cite id="443ea8f0-0">DFU care commonly uses digital photographic documentation with DUSS and WIfI scoring</cite>, and <cite id="443ea8f0-2">AI DFU systems analyze visible features (size, color, discoloration) captured by smartphone photos for early diagnosis and telemedicine sharing</cite>.

2) Smartphone wound imaging, measurement, and AI assistance
- Photo protocol and measurement: <cite id="69ce7e99-0">Studies from clinical sites used standardized smartphone photography (no zoom, macro settings, f/2.8 aperture, 30–40 cm distance, room light, no flash) by trained photographers to ensure accurate color/edge capture, with annotated DFU datasets for infection/ischemia regions of interest</cite>. <cite id="69ce7e99-1">Valid and reliable methods exist for visible DFU assessment in trained professionals; smartphone apps can measure wound area by tracing contours and comparing serial images</cite>.
- AI classification for risk signals: <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Visual cues for infection (redness, purulence) and ischemia (poor reperfusion, black gangrenous toes) can be learned by deep models to support early recognition and triage</cite>, and <cite id="443ea8f0-2">lightweight AI on smartphone photos can assist early DFU detection and guide prompt debridement and infection management</cite>. <cite id="69ce7e99-3">Grand Challenges like DFUC2020 built on ~4,000 real‑world images with bounding-box annotations to improve DFU detection accuracy for mobile deployment</cite>.
- Example apps/prototypes: <cite id="69ce7e99-2">DFU applications integrating multimedia education, thermal imaging (FLIR API) for temperature mapping, and wound area/depth estimation with secure backend (Firebase) for caregiver sharing</cite>. <cite id="69ce7e99-4">Training/eval datasets (2,000 train/2,000 test) from hospital acquisition reflect real‑world variability (distance, lighting, multiple ulcers, healing stages), with timestamps and rulers to improve robustness</cite>.

3) Offloading and footwear assessment apps
- Function: Categorize footwear, quantify plantar pressure hotspots, detect callus/moisture, and recommend offloading. <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Wearables and sensors can measure plantar pressure and foot temperature remotely, supporting offloading and reducing in‑person visits</cite>. <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">Guidelines emphasize appropriate footwear and skin care; mobile tools can prompt daily checks and capture deformities, calluses, or maceration for remote review</cite>.
- Implementation: Many programs tie into printable/customizable orthotics and sock therapy recommendations; some export pressure‑map snapshots to clinicians. Studies emphasize that <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">continuous observation and real‑time support improve early detection of complications</cite>, which includes offloading noncompliance or emerging pressure injuries.

4) Thermal imaging and infection/ischemia risk
- Thermal apps: <cite id="69ce7e99-2">Thermal imaging integrated into DFU apps can detect wound temperature gradients, estimate depth, and signal infection risk via hot/cold spots, with secure patient‑provider data sharing</cite>. 
- Clinical grounding: <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Infection and ischemia each occur in 40–80% and ~50% of DFUs, respectively; early recognition via visual cues (erythema, purulence for infection; poor reperfusion, gangrene for ischemia) underpins AI-assisted classification from photos</cite>. <cite id="443ea8f0-2">AI DFU detection systems can flag ischemia/infection risk from photographs to accelerate appropriate interventions</cite>.
- Practical protocol: <cite id="69ce7e99-0">For color/thermal imaging, standardized distance, lighting (no flash), and focus settings are critical to avoid artifacts and ensure clinically interpretable gradients</cite>.

5) Physiological and risk‑factor monitoring
- Remote vitals/chemistry: <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Sensors can track glucose levels and foot temperature; combined with plantar pressure mapping, they provide continuous observation and real‑time alerts</cite>. 
- Risk stratification tools: <cite id="443ea8f0-4">Validated scoring systems—DUSS, SINBAD, and University of Texas—quantify ulcer severity, ischemia, infection, and depth to predict healing and guide escalation; digital apps can prompt fields for these variables and auto‑generate summaries</cite>.

6) Education, reminders, and self-care support
- Behavior change: <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Mobile health tools improve knowledge and adherence to self-care practices, reducing incidence of new lesions</cite>. <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">Apps and wearables provide medication/reminders, foot exam prompts, and communication with clinicians, which aligns with IWGDF guidance to reduce severe complications</cite>.

How these apps perform on outcomes and adoption

- Healing and amputation: <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">Telemedicine cohorts show non‑inferior healing at 12 months, lower amputation, and no mortality difference versus usual care</cite>, while <cite id="6c7bedc4-4">a nurse‑led rural telemedicine trial found similar healing (32% vs 28%) and amputation (23% vs 25%) over 12 weeks</cite>. These trials indicate feasibility and comparable clinical outcomes; digital apps that embed these workflows can be expected to maintain similar non‑inferiority while improving adherence and early escalation, though effect sizes vary by implementation and population.
- Detection accuracy and usability: <cite id="69ce7e99-0">Clinically curated DFU photo datasets with expert annotations and standardized capture protocols demonstrate that smartphone photography yields accurate, reproducible color/texture data for DFU grading</cite>, and <cite id="69ce7e99-1">trained clinicians can reliably detect visible DFU changes with smartphone methods, supporting home monitoring</cite>. AI models trained on such data can assist grading but should be validated for device‑independent imaging quality and lighting conditions. <cite id="69ce7e99-4">Real‑world datasets capture distance, angle, and lighting variability, which is essential for robust deployment</cite>.
- Complication detection: <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Infection and ischemia can often be flagged by visual cues; deep models trained on wound photos can assist early detection and triage to reduce amputations</cite>. <cite id="443ea8f0-2">AI‑assisted DFU detection supports early debridement and infection management</cite>. <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Continuous observation and timely alerts can reduce severe complications</cite>.

Implementation and data-quality best practices

- Photo capture: <cite id="69ce7e99-0">Use consistent distance (30–40 cm), no zoom/macro, f/2.8 aperture, natural light without flash, and standardized body positioning; train users to avoid glare and focus on wound plane</cite>. Incorporate gridlines/level‑bubble guidance and timestamped photos with before/after comparison.
- Grading integration: <cite id="443ea8f0-0">Embed DUSS and WIfI score entry into the app to standardize severity capture</cite>, and <cite id="443ea8f0-4">include DUSS, SINBAD, and UT classification with explanations and thresholds for escalation</cite>. AI modules can generate preliminary risk flags for infection/ischemia for clinician review. <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Clinicians recognize infection via redness/purulence and ischemia via poor reperfusion/gangrene; models can be trained on these visual cues</cite>.
- Sensor/thermal workflows: <cite id="69ce7e99-2">For thermal apps, integrate FLIR‑class APIs and provide artifact‑resistance guidance (ambient light, distance, emissivity settings)</cite>. Map thermal hotspots to offloading recommendations and export to clinicians.
- Workflow orchestration: <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">Use push reminders for daily foot exams, medication adherence, and footwear checks; provide secure messaging to clinicians and caregiver sharing</cite>. <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Use telemedicine drop‑ins for biweekly triage, with remote de‑identification photo review and prescription of offloading, dressings, and labs</cite>.

Safety, limitations, and how to choose tools

- Variability and standardization: <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Heterogeneous designs and short follow‑ups limit generalizability; standardized outcome measures (healing time, infection, reulceration, amputation) are essential</cite>. <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">Future trials should be longer and include vulnerable subgroups</cite>. Clinically, <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">telemedicine is non‑inferior and reduces amputation</cite>, but <cite id="6c7bedc4-4">rural RCTs show similar amputation rates over shorter horizons</cite>; set expectations accordingly.
- AI reliability: <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Deep models can learn infection/ischemia cues but should be used as decision support; visual cues overlap and can be ambiguous, so clinician oversight is required</cite>. Validate models on multi‑vendor smartphones/cameras and lighting conditions, and institute second‑review thresholds for escalation.
- Tool selection checklist:
  - Core needs (photo docs, size/area, color/texture): Choose apps with standardized capture guidance and built‑in wound measurement/grading templates. <cite id="69ce7e99-1">Smartphone contour tracing and serial comparison are reliable for area trend assessment</cite>.
  - Infection/ischemia triage: Prefer tools with AI classifiers trained on DFU datasets and expert annotations. <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Visual cue libraries for infection vs ischemia</cite> and <cite id="69ce7e99-0">annotated ROIs for infection/ischemia</cite>.
  - Offloading/footwear: Favor apps with footwear assessment, callus/moisture detection, and exportable reports to clinicians, plus linkage to orthotic resources. <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Plantar pressure and temperature sensors support offloading</cite>.
  - Telemedicine tie‑in: Ensure two‑way clinician integration for escalation, with secure data handling and adherence tracking. <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">Telemedicine reduced amputation and was non‑inferior for healing</cite>.
  - Education/reminders: Select apps with tailored alerts per guideline domains (neuropathy education, footwear, skin care). <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">Guideline‑aligned prompts improve engagement and early complication detection</cite>.

Representative apps and platforms to pilot

- DFU remote care platforms: Telemedicine hubs with wound photo upload, grading forms (DUSS/SINBAD/UT), and clinician triage; pair with secure messaging and medication adherence tracking. <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">Telemedicine non‑inferiority and amputation reduction</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-4">similar outcomes in rural nurse‑led care</cite>.
- DFU imaging and AI: Apps combining high‑quality photo capture with AI overlays for infection/ischemia risk and area/deep‑ness estimation, with thermal imaging where available. <cite id="69ce7e99-0">Standardized photo capture and annotated datasets</cite>, <cite id="69ce7e99-2">thermal imaging plus area/depth estimation and secure sharing</cite>, and <cite id="443ea8f0-2">mobile AI for early DFU detection</cite>.
- Footwear/offloading apps: Programs that assess footwear pressure hotspots, recommend daily offloading routines, and link to printable orthotics; export pressure snapshots to clinicians. <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Sensors and wearables monitor plantar pressure and foot temperature for remote support</cite>.
- Education/reminders: Apps that deliver daily prompts for foot inspection, moisturizing, nail trimming, footwear checks, and medication adherence with symptom escalation pathways. <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">mHealth improves knowledge and reduces new lesions</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">aligns with IWGDF self‑care priorities</cite>.

Putting it together: a DFU assessment and monitoring stack

1) Baseline assessment on day 0:
- In-clinic or first visit: smartphone photos with structured DUSS/SINBAD/UT scoring; optional thermal imaging; plantar pressure mapping; glucose trend review. <cite id="443ea8f0-0">DUSS and WIfI scoring capture severity and ischemia/infection</cite>, <cite id="443ea8f0-4">SINBAD and UT classify ulcer features to predict outcomes</cite>, <cite id="69ce7e99-0">standardized photography yields clinically interpretable color/texture</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">sensors provide foot temperature and plantar pressure data</cite>.
2) At-home monitoring (daily to weekly):
- Photo docs with AI overlays (infection/ischemia flags) and wound area trend; thermal snapshots; foot exam reminders; footwear/callus checks; symptom escalation to clinician. <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Visual cue–based AI assists early recognition</cite>, <cite id="69ce7e99-1">smartphone area measurement and serial comparison</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">continuous observation enables early detection</cite>.
3) Telemedicine triage (biweekly):
- Secure video consults with photo review, adjust offloading/dressings, schedule in‑person if needed. <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">Telemedicine achieved non‑inferior healing and reduced amputation</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-4">nurse‑led telemedicine matched usual care in rural settings</cite>.

Practical tips and pitfalls

- Workflow fidelity: <cite id="69ce7e99-0">Adhere to standardized photography (distance, aperture, lighting, no flash) to avoid misinterpretation of color/gradients</cite>. Provide checklists and training videos.
- AI governance: <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Use AI outputs as advisory flags; require clinician review before escalation</cite>. Maintain audit trails and allow expert override.
- Sensor hygiene: Calibrate thermal cameras and validate smartphone camera consistency; document device models and settings in reports.
- Continuous improvement: <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Collect standardized outcomes (time to reulceration, infection, amputation) to refine algorithms and protocols</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">align updates with guideline revisions</cite>.

Bottom line
- Apps that combine structured DFU grading, standardized smartphone imaging, AI-assisted risk flags for infection/ischemia, offloading/footwear assessment, and telemedicine triage are supported by evidence for non‑inferior clinical outcomes and improved complication detection, with careful attention to data quality and clinician oversight. <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">Telemedicine reduced amputation and was non‑inferior for healing at 12 months</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">mobile self‑care tools improve knowledge and adherence and can reduce new lesions</cite>. <cite id="6c7bedc4-4">In rural trials, telemedicine achieved outcomes comparable to usual care, supporting scalable deployment</cite>. For the best results, pair validated grading workflows (DUSS/SINBAD/UT) with standardized imaging protocols and secure clinician integration, and use AI as a decision‑support layer for early detection of infection and ischemia. <cite id="443ea8f0-4">Validated scoring systems predict outcomes and guide escalation</cite>, and <cite id="443ea8f0-1">AI models trained on wound visual cues can accelerate recognition of red flags</cite>.

Title: Effectiveness of Telemedicine for the Management of Foot Ulcers in People With Diabetes: A Meta-Analysis
Snippet: Treatment of diabetes-related foot ulcers presents great pressure on the healthcare system in terms of management strategy and allocation of resources. Telemedicine can be used to treat diabetic foot ulcers more effectively. This meta-analysis aims to evaluate the impacts of telemedicine on the treatment of diabetic foot ulcers. The current meta-analysis was conducted as per the reported guidelines of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) statement. Two reviewers independently searched for relevant articles using PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews from inception to 31 August 2022, assessing the impacts of telemedicine on the treatment of diabetic foot ulcers. The primary outcomes assessed in the current meta-analysis included the percentage of foot ulcers healed and the time of healing foot ulcers within 12 months. Secondary outcomes included the percentage of amputation (minor and major) and all-cause mortality. A total of six studies were included in the current meta-analysis enrolling 1876 patients with diabetic foot ulcers. No difference was there between the two groups in terms of the number of patients whose ulcer healed (risk ratio (RR): 1.01, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.93-1.09), time to healing of wound within 12 months (mean difference: -0.07, 95% CI: -0.31-0.17), the incidence of amputation (RR: 0.73, 95% CI: 0.54-1.00), and all-cause mortality (RR: 0.99, 95% CI: 0.42-2.37). In conclusion, the study found that telemedicine is non-inferior to standard care in terms of reducing healing time and the number of patients with ulcer healing within 12 months. The study also found that the incidence of amputation is also lower in patients assigned to the telemedicine group compared to patients in the control group and no significant differences were reported in terms of mortality.

These devices allow for the control of foot temperature, glucose levels, and plantar pressure, facilitating remote treatment and reducing the need for in-person consultation [7]. The integration of artificial intelligence and digital communication provides personalized and timely management of foot ulcer. Title: Telemedical treatment of diabetic foot ulcer in rural and remote areas: a prospective single centre randomised controlled clinical trial
Snippet: The role of telemedical treatment for patients with diabetic foot ulcers residing in rural areas remains uncertain. Therefore, our objective was to conduct a randomized controlled trial comparing the effectiveness of telemedical treatment in rural settings with the standard tertiary healthcare approach for managing diabetic foot ulcers. Title: Sustainable AI for diabetic foot ulcer detection: a deep learning approach for early diagnosis
Snippet: The potential of smart sensors in healthcare and medical applications has significantly increased because to recent advancements in wearable technology, sensors, and electrical components. The advancement of these technologies has greatly aided in diagnosing diabetic foot ulcers among other applications across numerous industries. Thus, this proposed system provides mobile application to diagnosis DFU skin against normal skin. At the Lancashie Teaching Hospitals, diabetic foot ulcer footprints were taken a few years ago. They used three different digital cameras to take pictures of the footprints: a Nikon D300 with 24.2 megapixels, a Kodak DX530 with 5 megapixels, and a Nikon COLPIX P100 (10.3 megapixel). The images were captured by using autofocus without any zoom, macro settings, and an aperture setting of f/2.8 at approximately 30 to 40 cms from the appropriate point of the wound plane. Flashlight has not been used as the primary source of illumination; rather, only the lights within the room were allowed to be used. There are four main types of chronic wounds: pressure ulcers, diabetic foot ulcers, venous ulcers, and arterial ulcers. Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs), the focus of this paper, are a major complication of diabetes. Infection and ischemia are two common problems that occur in the healing process of DFUs, which may lead to amputation of limbs and admission of patients into hospitals [6]. After limb amputation, the patient's quality of life degrades quickly with a life expectancy of fewer than 3 years thereafter [7]. Infection occurs in 40%-80% [8] of DFUs and ischemia occurs in almost 50% of DFUs [9]. Infection is caused by the presence of bacteria in the wound, which causes cell death. DFUs are at risk of becoming infected as they are often located on the lower limbs such as on the sole of the patient's foot [10]. Ischemia is caused by insufficient blood circulation due to chronic complications of diabetes. It is essential to recognize infection and ischemia of DFUs early to reduce the risk of amputation. The economic burden of treating DFUs including infection and ischemia, ranges from $9-13 billion [11]. 

To diagnose infection and ischemia accurately, the wound bacteriology needs to be tested combined with review of patient records such as clinical history, physical health and blood tests. But this information is not always available to clinicians. Experienced wound experts are able to recognize the presence of infection and ischemia in DFUs by visual inspection. Visual cues of wound infection include increased redness in and around the ulcer, and colored purulent. Visual cues for a wound with ischemia include the presence of poor reperfusion to the foot, or black gangrenous toes (tissue death to part of the foot).
</snippet>

Snippet: A significant consequence of diabetes mellitus, diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) affect millions of individuals across the globe [1]. These ulcers pose a significant public health risk, leading to morbidity, amputations, and mortality. Factors including neuropathy, ischemia, and infection delay the healing process, resulting in the formation of these ulcers [2]. DFUs have a substantial impact on individuals' quality of life [3]. Individuals with chronic wounds generally experience intense pain, restricted movement, and a lack of social interaction [4]. These wounds require extended medical consultations, dressing changes, and occasionally surgery interventions. Due to their limited physical ability and dependency on caretakers, individuals encounter depression and anxiety [5]. Hospitalization or amputations may increase the length of stay and cause substantial healthcare expenses. 

Effective DFU therapy requires timely and precise ischemia and infection identification [6]. Traditionally, DFUs diagnosis relied on laboratory testing, imaging, and clinical evaluations [7]. Clinicians identify infections using clinical symptoms, bacterial cultures, and inflammatory markers, whereas perfusion levels determine ischemia. The dependence on clinical knowledge renders these procedures laborious, subjective, and inconsistent. Imaging modalities, including thermal, hyperspectral, and fluorescence imaging have gained traction in diagnosing DFUs in the initial stages [8]. These modalities offer detailed insights into blood flow, tissue composition, and infection biomarkers [9]. However, extensive implementation costs and a steep learning curve for healthcare professionals prevent the widespread adoption of these modalities. In contrast, photographic images capture visible wound features, including size, shape, and discoloration, with sufficient clarity [10]. These features can be shared for telemedicine consultations, supporting early DFUs diagnosis. 

In the absence of prompt medical attention, ulcers have the potential to penetrate deep into soft tissue, tendons, and potentially bone, elevating the likelihood of developing osteomyelitis and systemic infections leading to the amputation of the lower extremities [10]. By using an artificial intelligence-powered DFUs detection system, healthcare personnel may initiate debridement and infection management in the early stages, preventing severe consequences [11].
</snippet>

Snippet: One of the complications of diabetes is diabetic foot ulcers (DFU) that can result in the removal of a foot or limb (Alzubaidi et al., 2020c). Commonly, the DFU is situated on the heel, and symptoms often include dry cracks, leg pain, foot swelling, skin temperature differences, and skin color changes. The cost of DFU treatment is usually high, and mortality rates increase if the condition is not treated at an early stage. The critical parameters for predicting the DFU's amputation risk or healing potential are detecting and diagnosing the infection or areas of ischemia (Tulloch, Zamani & Akrami, 2020). Chronic diabetes in the human body causes poor blood circulation that in turn causes ischemia (Everett & Mathioudakis, 2018). Therefore, palpating the pulses of blood flow in the foot can help discover ischemia (Amin et al., 2020), and poor foot reperfusion, which could develop into a DFU infection, shows the ischemia visually (Peter-Riesch, 2016). 

From the researchers' point of view, detecting the DFU is the objective, as (a) the appearance of DFU can change in terms of location, shape, and size, (b) resemblances between intra-and inter-class variations, and (c) lighting conditions. It should be noted that there are comprehensive, in-depth medical studies relating to leg blood vessels, blood tests, bacteriological studies, and physical examinations. However, these tests and resources are often inaccessible worldwide. This paper used a combination of two DFU datasets: (Goyal et al., 2018;Alzubaidi et al., 2020c). The first one (Goyal et al., 2018) contained 1,610 patches taken from foot images. These patches were divided into two classes: normal, with 641 patches, and abnormal, with 969 patches. The second dataset (Alzubaidi et al., 2020c) contained 1,477 patches taken from foot images, with 742 classified as normal and 735 abnormal, to provide a total of 3,087 patches.

Title: Reliability and Validation of Three Scoring Systems in the Assessment of Diabetic Foot Ulcers
Snippet: A diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) is defined as an ulceration of the foot associated with neuropathy, varying degrees of ischemia, and infection [1]. It is estimated that around 19% to 34% of patients with diabetes may develop a foot ulcer during their lifetime [2]. Diabetic foot ulcer represents one of the most serious and debilitating complications of diabetes mellitus [2]. The five-year risk of mortality for a patient with a diabetic foot ulcer is 2.5 times higher than that for a patient without a foot ulcer [2]. With such a high level of morbidity resulting from debilitating osteomyelitis and amputation in patients with DFU, it is of utmost importance to properly address and treat the underlying causes of the condition [3]. 

The sites of ulcers in diabetes are typically located in areas of the foot exposed to constant pressure or repetitive trauma [4]. Diabetic foot ulcers arise from a complex interplay of factors such as prolonged duration of diabetes, poor glycaemic control, inadequate foot care, structural foot deformities, dry skin, and repeated shear stress on the diabetic foot, leading to callus formation and subsequent ulceration [5]. These ulcers not only compromise quality of life but also significantly increase the risk of infection, hospitalization, and lower limb amputation [6]. 

Early identification of high-risk patients is therefore critical, and simple screening tools used by primary care physicians and paramedical staff can play a pivotal role in reducing morbidity and mortality [7]. Several scoring systems, including the Diabetic Ulcer Severity Score (DUSS), the Site, Ischemia, Neuropathy, Bacterial Infection, Area, and Depth (SINBAD) classification, and the University of Texas wound classification system (UT classification), have been developed to assess ulcer severity and predict outcomes [8][9][10]. Comparing these scoring systems can provide valuable insights into their relative effectiveness in forecasting wound healing in patients with DFU [11].

Below is a practical, evidence-backed overview of mobile apps and digital tools for assessing and monitoring diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs), organized by function and supported by clinical/technology studies.

Why digital tools matter for DFUs
- DFUs impose high healthcare use and risk; early detection, frequent monitoring, and timely escalation are key to avoiding amputation and hospitalization. <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">Telemedicine for DFUs was non‑inferior to usual care for healing within 12 months, reduced amputation, and showed no mortality difference</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">mobile tools can enhance self‑care, remote monitoring, and early complication detection</cite>. However, <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">variability in study designs and outcomes limits firm effect size comparisons</cite> and <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">more standardized, long‑term trials are needed</cite>.
- Digital workflows align with guideline recommendations: <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">IWGDF emphasizes patient education, regular foot examination, footwear care, and skin care, which map to mobile app features and telehealth triage</cite>.

Core categories of DFU apps and representative tools

1) Telemedicine and remote wound assessment platforms
- Function: Secure video consults, photo documentation, guided questionnaires, clinician triage, and care-plan tracking. They enable routine follow‑up, early detection of worsening, and reduced in‑person load. <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">Telemedicine reduced amputation risk and was non‑inferior for healing at 12 months vs usual care</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-4">a rural RCT found similar healing (32% vs 28%) and amputation rates (23% vs 25%) between nurse‑led telemedicine and usual care over 12 weeks</cite>. 
- Integration tips: Many platforms pair smartphone photos with structured grading. <cite id="443ea8f0-0">DFU care commonly uses digital photographic documentation with DUSS and WIfI scoring</cite>, and <cite id="443ea8f0-2">AI DFU systems analyze visible features (size, color, discoloration) captured by smartphone photos for early diagnosis and telemedicine sharing</cite>.

2) Smartphone wound imaging, measurement, and AI assistance
- Photo protocol and measurement: <cite id="69ce7e99-0">Studies from clinical sites used standardized smartphone photography (no zoom, macro settings, f/2.8 aperture, 30–40 cm distance, room light, no flash) by trained photographers to ensure accurate color/edge capture, with annotated DFU datasets for infection/ischemia regions of interest</cite>. <cite id="69ce7e99-1">Valid and reliable methods exist for visible DFU assessment in trained professionals; smartphone apps can measure wound area by tracing contours and comparing serial images</cite>.
- AI classification for risk signals: <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Visual cues for infection (redness, purulence) and ischemia (poor reperfusion, black gangrenous toes) can be learned by deep models to support early recognition and triage</cite>, and <cite id="443ea8f0-2">lightweight AI on smartphone photos can assist early DFU detection and guide prompt debridement and infection management</cite>. <cite id="69ce7e99-3">Grand Challenges like DFUC2020 built on ~4,000 real‑world images with bounding-box annotations to improve DFU detection accuracy for mobile deployment</cite>.
- Example apps/prototypes: <cite id="69ce7e99-2">DFU applications integrating multimedia education, thermal imaging (FLIR API) for temperature mapping, and wound area/depth estimation with secure backend (Firebase) for caregiver sharing</cite>. <cite id="69ce7e99-4">Training/eval datasets (2,000 train/2,000 test) from hospital acquisition reflect real‑world variability (distance, lighting, multiple ulcers, healing stages), with timestamps and rulers to improve robustness</cite>.

3) Offloading and footwear assessment apps
- Function: Categorize footwear, quantify plantar pressure hotspots, detect callus/moisture, and recommend offloading. <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Wearables and sensors can measure plantar pressure and foot temperature remotely, supporting offloading and reducing in‑person visits</cite>. <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">Guidelines emphasize appropriate footwear and skin care; mobile tools can prompt daily checks and capture deformities, calluses, or maceration for remote review</cite>.
- Implementation: Many programs tie into printable/customizable orthotics and sock therapy recommendations; some export pressure‑map snapshots to clinicians. Studies emphasize that <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">continuous observation and real‑time support improve early detection of complications</cite>, which includes offloading noncompliance or emerging pressure injuries.

4) Thermal imaging and infection/ischemia risk
- Thermal apps: <cite id="69ce7e99-2">Thermal imaging integrated into DFU apps can detect wound temperature gradients, estimate depth, and signal infection risk via hot/cold spots, with secure patient‑provider data sharing</cite>. 
- Clinical grounding: <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Infection and ischemia each occur in 40–80% and ~50% of DFUs, respectively; early recognition via visual cues (erythema, purulence for infection; poor reperfusion, gangrene for ischemia) underpins AI-assisted classification from photos</cite>. <cite id="443ea8f0-2">AI DFU detection systems can flag ischemia/infection risk from photographs to accelerate appropriate interventions</cite>.
- Practical protocol: <cite id="69ce7e99-0">For color/thermal imaging, standardized distance, lighting (no flash), and focus settings are critical to avoid artifacts and ensure clinically interpretable gradients</cite>.

5) Physiological and risk‑factor monitoring
- Remote vitals/chemistry: <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Sensors can track glucose levels and foot temperature; combined with plantar pressure mapping, they provide continuous observation and real‑time alerts</cite>. 
- Risk stratification tools: <cite id="443ea8f0-4">Validated scoring systems—DUSS, SINBAD, and University of Texas—quantify ulcer severity, ischemia, infection, and depth to predict healing and guide escalation; digital apps can prompt fields for these variables and auto‑generate summaries</cite>.

6) Education, reminders, and self-care support
- Behavior change: <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Mobile health tools improve knowledge and adherence to self-care practices, reducing incidence of new lesions</cite>. <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">Apps and wearables provide medication/reminders, foot exam prompts, and communication with clinicians, which aligns with IWGDF guidance to reduce severe complications</cite>.

How these apps perform on outcomes and adoption

- Healing and amputation: <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">Telemedicine cohorts show non‑inferior healing at 12 months, lower amputation, and no mortality difference versus usual care</cite>, while <cite id="6c7bedc4-4">a nurse‑led rural telemedicine trial found similar healing (32% vs 28%) and amputation (23% vs 25%) over 12 weeks</cite>. These trials indicate feasibility and comparable clinical outcomes; digital apps that embed these workflows can be expected to maintain similar non‑inferiority while improving adherence and early escalation, though effect sizes vary by implementation and population.
- Detection accuracy and usability: <cite id="69ce7e99-0">Clinically curated DFU photo datasets with expert annotations and standardized capture protocols demonstrate that smartphone photography yields accurate, reproducible color/texture data for DFU grading</cite>, and <cite id="69ce7e99-1">trained clinicians can reliably detect visible DFU changes with smartphone methods, supporting home monitoring</cite>. AI models trained on such data can assist grading but should be validated for device‑independent imaging quality and lighting conditions. <cite id="69ce7e99-4">Real‑world datasets capture distance, angle, and lighting variability, which is essential for robust deployment</cite>.
- Complication detection: <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Infection and ischemia can often be flagged by visual cues; deep models trained on wound photos can assist early detection and triage to reduce amputations</cite>. <cite id="443ea8f0-2">AI‑assisted DFU detection supports early debridement and infection management</cite>. <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Continuous observation and timely alerts can reduce severe complications</cite>.

Implementation and data-quality best practices

- Photo capture: <cite id="69ce7e99-0">Use consistent distance (30–40 cm), no zoom/macro, f/2.8 aperture, natural light without flash, and standardized body positioning; train users to avoid glare and focus on wound plane</cite>. - Grading integration: <cite id="443ea8f0-0">Embed DUSS and WIfI score entry into the app to standardize severity capture</cite>, and <cite id="443ea8f0-4">include DUSS, SINBAD, and UT classification with explanations and thresholds for escalation</cite>. AI modules can generate preliminary risk flags for infection/ischemia for clinician review. <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Clinicians recognize infection via redness/purulence and ischemia via poor reperfusion/gangrene; models can be trained on these visual cues</cite>.
- Sensor/thermal workflows: <cite id="69ce7e99-2">For thermal apps, integrate FLIR‑class APIs and provide artifact‑resistance guidance (ambient light, distance, emissivity settings)</cite>. Map thermal hotspots to offloading recommendations and export to clinicians.
- Workflow orchestration: <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">Use push reminders for daily foot exams, medication adherence, and footwear checks; provide secure messaging to clinicians and caregiver sharing</cite>. <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Use telemedicine drop‑ins for biweekly triage, with remote de‑identification photo review and prescription of offloading, dressings, and labs</cite>.

Safety, limitations, and how to choose tools

- Variability and standardization: <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Heterogeneous designs and short follow‑ups limit generalizability; standardized outcome measures (healing time, infection, reulceration, amputation) are essential</cite>. <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">Future trials should be longer and include vulnerable subgroups</cite>. Clinically, <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">telemedicine is non‑inferior and reduces amputation</cite>, but <cite id="6c7bedc4-4">rural RCTs show similar amputation rates over shorter horizons</cite>; set expectations accordingly.
- AI reliability: <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Deep models can learn infection/ischemia cues but should be used as decision support; visual cues overlap and can be ambiguous, so clinician oversight is required</cite>. Validate models on multi‑vendor smartphones/cameras and lighting conditions, and institute second‑review thresholds for escalation.
- Tool selection checklist:
  - Core needs (photo docs, size/area, color/texture): Choose apps with standardized capture guidance and built‑in wound measurement/grading templates. <cite id="69ce7e99-1">Smartphone contour tracing and serial comparison are reliable for area trend assessment</cite>.
  - Infection/ischemia triage: Prefer tools with AI classifiers trained on DFU datasets and expert annotations. <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Visual cue libraries for infection vs ischemia</cite> and <cite id="69ce7e99-0">annotated ROIs for infection/ischemia</cite>.
  - Offloading/footwear: Favor apps with footwear assessment, callus/moisture detection, and exportable reports to clinicians, plus linkage to orthotic resources. <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Plantar pressure and temperature sensors support offloading</cite>.
  - Telemedicine tie‑in: Ensure two‑way clinician integration for escalation, with secure data handling and adherence tracking. <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">Telemedicine reduced amputation and was non‑inferior for healing</cite>.
  - Education/reminders: Select apps with tailored alerts per guideline domains (neuropathy education, footwear, skin care). <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">Guideline‑aligned prompts improve engagement and early complication detection</cite>.

Representative apps and platforms to pilot

- DFU remote care platforms: Telemedicine hubs with wound photo upload, grading forms (DUSS/SINBAD/UT), and clinician triage; pair with secure messaging and medication adherence tracking. <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">Telemedicine non‑inferiority and amputation reduction</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-4">similar outcomes in rural nurse‑led care</cite>.
- DFU imaging and AI: Apps combining high‑quality photo capture with AI overlays for infection/ischemia risk and area/deep‑ness estimation, with thermal imaging where available. <cite id="69ce7e99-0">Standardized photo capture and annotated datasets</cite>, <cite id="69ce7e99-2">thermal imaging plus area/depth estimation and secure sharing</cite>, and <cite id="443ea8f0-2">mobile AI for early DFU detection</cite>.
- Footwear/offloading apps: Programs that assess footwear pressure hotspots, recommend daily offloading routines, and link to printable orthotics; export pressure snapshots to clinicians. <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Sensors and wearables monitor plantar pressure and foot temperature for remote support</cite>.
- Education/reminders: Apps that deliver daily prompts for foot inspection, moisturizing, nail trimming, footwear checks, and medication adherence with symptom escalation pathways. <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">mHealth improves knowledge and reduces new lesions</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">aligns with IWGDF self‑care priorities</cite>.

Putting it together: a DFU assessment and monitoring stack

1) Baseline assessment on day 0:
- In-clinic or first visit: smartphone photos with structured DUSS/SINBAD/UT scoring; optional thermal imaging; plantar pressure mapping; glucose trend review. <cite id="443ea8f0-0">DUSS and WIfI scoring capture severity and ischemia/infection</cite>, <cite id="443ea8f0-4">SINBAD and UT classify ulcer features to predict outcomes</cite>, <cite id="69ce7e99-0">standardized photography yields clinically interpretable color/texture</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">sensors provide foot temperature and plantar pressure data</cite>.
2) At-home monitoring (daily to weekly):
- Photo docs with AI overlays (infection/ischemia flags) and wound area trend; thermal snapshots; foot exam reminders; footwear/callus checks; symptom escalation to clinician. <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Visual cue–based AI assists early recognition</cite>, <cite id="69ce7e99-1">smartphone area measurement and serial comparison</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">continuous observation enables early detection</cite>.
3) Telemedicine triage (biweekly):
- Secure video consults with photo review, adjust offloading/dressings, schedule in‑person if needed. <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">Telemedicine achieved non‑inferior healing and reduced amputation</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-4">nurse‑led telemedicine matched usual care in rural settings</cite>.

Practical tips and pitfalls

- Workflow fidelity: <cite id="69ce7e99-0">Adhere to standardized photography (distance, aperture, lighting, no flash) to avoid misinterpretation of color/gradients</cite>. Provide checklists and training videos.
- AI governance: <cite id="443ea8f0-1">Use AI outputs as advisory flags; require clinician review before escalation</cite>. Maintain audit trails and allow expert override.
- Sensor hygiene: Calibrate thermal cameras and validate smartphone camera consistency; document device models and settings in reports.
- Continuous improvement: <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">Collect standardized outcomes (time to reulceration, infection, amputation) to refine algorithms and protocols</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-3">align updates with guideline revisions</cite>.

Bottom line
- Apps that combine structured DFU grading, standardized smartphone imaging, AI-assisted risk flags for infection/ischemia, offloading/footwear assessment, and telemedicine triage are supported by evidence for non‑inferior clinical outcomes and improved complication detection, with careful attention to data quality and clinician oversight. <cite id="6c7bedc4-0">Telemedicine reduced amputation and was non‑inferior for healing at 12 months</cite>, and <cite id="6c7bedc4-2">mobile self‑care tools improve knowledge and adherence and can reduce new lesions</cite>. <cite id="6c7bedc4-4">In rural trials, telemedicine achieved outcomes comparable to usual care, supporting scalable deployment</cite>. For the best results, pair validated grading workflows (DUSS/SINBAD/UT) with standardized imaging protocols and secure clinician integration, and use AI as a decision‑support layer for early detection of infection and ischemia. <cite id="443ea8f0-4">Validated scoring systems predict outcomes and guide escalation</cite>, and <cite id="443ea8f0-1">AI models trained on wound visual cues can accelerate recognition of red flags</cite>. </answer>

Title: Effectiveness of Telemedicine for the Management of Foot Ulcers in People With Diabetes: A Meta-Analysis
Snippet: Treatment of diabetes-related foot ulcers presents great pressure on the healthcare system in terms of management strategy and allocation of resources. Telemedicine can be used to treat diabetic foot ulcers more effectively. This meta-analysis aims to evaluate the impacts of telemedicine on the treatment of diabetic foot ulcers. The current meta-analysis was conducted as per the reported guidelines of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) statement. Two reviewers independently searched for relevant articles using PubMed, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews from inception to 31 August 2022, assessing the impacts of telemedicine on the treatment of diabetic foot ulcers. The primary outcomes assessed in the current meta-analysis included the percentage of foot ulcers healed and the time of healing foot ulcers within 12 months. Secondary outcomes included the percentage of amputation (minor and major) and all-cause mortality. A total of six studies were included in the current meta-analysis enrolling 1876 patients with diabetic foot ulcers. No difference was there between the two groups in terms of the number of patients whose ulcer healed (risk ratio (RR): 1.01, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.93-1.09), time to healing of wound within 12 months (mean difference: -0.07, 95% CI: -0.31-0.17), the incidence of amputation (RR: 0.73, 95% CI: 0.54-1.00), and all-cause mortality (RR: 0.99, 95% CI: 0.42-2.37). In conclusion, the study found that telemedicine is non-inferior to standard care in terms of reducing healing time and the number of patients with ulcer healing within 12 months. The study also found that the incidence of amputation is also lower in patients assigned to the telemedicine group compared to patients in the control group and no significant differences were reported in terms of mortality.

Snippet: In recent years, various technologies, including mobile applications, wearable sensors, and telemedicine platforms, have been developed to enhance adherence to self-care practices and facilitate the early detection of complications. Self-care is essential for preventing and managing complications of diabetic foot ulcers [10]. Innovative technologies such as sensors and portable devices have significantly improved medical monitoring by offering continuous observation and real-time support. These devices allow for the control of foot temperature, glucose levels, and plantar pressure, facilitating remote treatment and reducing the need for in-person consultation [7]. The integration of artificial intelligence and digital communication provides personalized and timely management of foot ulcer. Advances in these areas have empowered patients to engage in self-care and offer innovative solutions to prevent complications [11]. 

The emergence of mobile health technologies ( [12,13]), presents a promising avenue for enhancing self-care practices among patients with chronic conditions, including diabetes. Their study categorized mobile applications based on their purpose, such as providing information on nutrition and diet, facilitating the measurement of physiological parameters, offering medication reminders, and underscoring their potential to improve patient engagement and adherence to treatment plans. 

Throughout this review, the term "diabetic foot ulcer" (DFU) is used as a broader construct encompassing foot complications arising from diabetes. However, the more clinically specific term "diabetic foot ulcer" (DFU) is widely adopted in the literature and is often the primary focus of digital interventions aimed at improving selfcare and preventing complications. For clarity and alignment with the standard terminology, DFU will be used when referring specifically to ulcerative complications. 

According to the IWGDF 2023 definition, a diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) is a full-thickness wound located below the ankle in a person with diabetes, often resulting from neuropathy and peripheral arterial disease. Title: Telemedical treatment of diabetic foot ulcer in rural and remote areas: a prospective single centre randomised controlled clinical trial
Snippet: The role of telemedical treatment for patients with diabetic foot ulcers residing in rural areas remains uncertain. Therefore, our objective was to conduct a randomized controlled trial comparing the effectiveness of telemedical treatment in rural settings with the standard tertiary healthcare approach for managing diabetic foot ulcers. The study was conducted between 2016 and 2022. Participants were randomly assigned 2:1 to either face-to-face usual care (UC) group or telemedical treatment group. The protocol for the telemedical treatment group involved fortnightly consultations conducted by a locally trained nurse in the patients’ rural hospital over 12 weeks compared to similar protocol for face-to-face podiatrist-treated UC group. The primary endpoints were complete healing of the ulcer or limb amputation while secondary outcomes included circulating markers of inflammation as a marker of wound healing. One hundred and fifty-one participants out of 232 met the inclusion criteria and 50 were randomised to telemedical treatment group and 101 to the UC group. The clinical and demographic characteristics of the participants were similar in both groups. Following 12 weeks of treatment, we observed that complete ulcer healing was achieved in 16 out of 50 individuals (32%) in the telemedical treatment group, while 28 out of 101 individuals (28%) in the UC group achieved the same outcome (p = 0.58). Amputation rates were 23% (11/50) in the telemedicine and 25% (23/101) in the UC group (p = 0.080). This promising result suggests that telemedicine could be a viable option for rural patients; however, further research exploring other clinically relevant endpoints and vulnerable subgroups is needed to solidify its role. Title: Sustainable AI for diabetic foot ulcer detection: a deep learning approach for early diagnosis
Snippet: The potential of smart sensors in healthcare and medical applications has significantly increased because to recent advancements in wearable technology, sensors, and electrical components. The advancement of these technologies has greatly aided in diagnosing diabetic foot ulcers among other applications across numerous industries. Thus, this proposed system provides mobile application to diagnosis DFU skin against normal skin. At the Lancashie Teaching Hospitals, diabetic foot ulcer footprints were taken a few years ago. They used three different digital cameras to take pictures of the footprints: a Nikon D300 with 24.2 megapixels, a Kodak DX530 with 5 megapixels, and a Nikon COLPIX P100 (10.3 megapixel). The images were captured by using autofocus without any zoom, macro settings, and an aperture setting of f/2.8 at approximately 30 to 40 cms from the appropriate point of the wound plane. Flashlight has not been used as the primary source of illumination; rather, only the lights within the room were allowed to be used. This was done to ensure that the finished photographs had accurate color reproduction. These photographs were taken by medical photographers who are familiar with digital field unification and have more than five years of experience in the field of physician photography. During the preliminary stage of the processing, poor-quality photographs were discarded, and released duplicates were avoided based on each file's unique hash code. Manchester Metropolitan University and the Lancashire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust provide access to digital DFU photo files that include annotations from medical practitioners [12]. The sharing of these findings is intended to motivate more scholars to conduct replicated studies in this field. There are three sorts of publicly accessible datasets that are available in academics. The first dataset consists of foot skin patches for the classification of wounds [13], the second dataset consists of regions of interest for the classification of infection and ischemia [14], and the third dataset is the most recent one made available for DFU detection.

Title: Empowering Diabetes Patient with Mobile Health Technologies
Snippet: Diabetic foot is a main cause for nontraumatic lower limb amputation and precedes 85% of the cases. Approximately 15% of diabetes patients will develop diabetic foot ulcers in their lifetime [99]. It is recommended for all diabetes patients to perform annual extensive foot examination to identify risk factors predictive of foot ulcers. Patient should be screened for signs of peripheral neuropathy and peripheral vascular disease, simultaneously paying attention to identify other risk factors such as foot deformities, past foot ulcers, visual impairment, and cigarette smoking [97]. Currently, researched mHealth method to facilitate foot care is using high quality photography to diagnose foot ulcers and preulcerative lesions. Trained professional can diagnose visible diabetic foot changes in valid and reliable manner, which implies methods usability as a monitoring tool in home environment [100]. Originally developed was a method for wound area measurement. The wound margins are recognized with the help of smartphone. First, the wound contour is copied on the foil. The area is then measured with smartphone app and compared with previous measurements [101].

Title: Usability Of “DFU Application” For Diabetic Foot Ulcer Prevention
Snippet: The DFU mobile application was developed as an mHealth tool to provide education on diabetic foot ulcer prevention and management. The app integrates multimedia educational modules with thermal imaging capabilities to detect wound temperature, estimate wound depth and area, and support early infection risk detection. Photographs from both left and right extremities are used to quantify ulcer characteristics and provide feedback to users and caregivers. The application was built using Android Studio with Java and Kotlin programming languages and integrates a thermal imaging API compatible with FLIR sensors. A Firebase backend was used for data storage and authentication, ensuring secure and real-time access for both users and healthcare providers (Figure 1).

Title: DFUC2020: Analysis Towards Diabetic Foot Ulcer Detection
Snippet: Wounds on the feet known as Diabetic Foot Ulcers (DFUs) are a major complication of diabetes because they can become infected, leading to amputation of the foot or lower limb. In previous studies, various researchers [1][2][3][4] [5] have achieved high accuracy in the recognition of DFUs using machine learning algorithms. Additionally, researchers have demonstrated proof-of-concept in studies using mobile devices for foot image capture [6] and DFU detection [7]. However, there are still gaps in implementing these technologies across multiple devices and locations in real-world settings. To bridge these gaps, we bring world-leading researchers from international institutions to work collaboratively towards automatic DFU detection. 

The goal of the Diabetic Foot Ulcers Grand Challenge 2020 (DFUC 2020) [8] is to improve the accuracy of DFU detection in a real-world setting, and to motivate the use of more advanced machine learning techniques that are datadriven in nature. In turn, this will aid the development of a mobile app that can be used by patients, their carers, or their family members to help with remote detection and monitoring of DFU in a home setting.

Title: DFUCare: deep learning platform for diabetic foot ulcer detection, analysis, and monitoring
Snippet: The goal of the Diabetic Foot Ulcer Competition 2020 (DFUC 2020) dataset was to improve the accuracy of DFU detection in real-world settings (18). The dataset consisted of foot images with DFUs collected from Lancashire Teaching Hospitals. The images were captured using three digital cameras (Kodak DX4530, Nikon D3300 and Nikon COOLPIX P100), and close-ups of the foot were taken without zoom or macro functions. The dataset comprised of 4,000 images, with 2,000 used for training and 2000 for testing. The images were acquired during regular patient appointments, resulting in variability in factors such as distance, angle, lighting, and the presence of background objects. The dataset included cases with multiple DFUs, different stages of healing, partial foot visibility, and foot deformities. The dataset also featured cases with time stamps, rulers, and partial blurring or obfuscation of wounds. The images were annotated by healthcare professionals, indicating the ulcer location using bounding boxes.

The advancement of these technologies has greatly aided in diagnosing diabetic foot ulcers among other applications across numerous industries. Thus, this proposed system provides mobile application to diagnosis DFU skin against normal skin. At the Lancashie Teaching Hospitals, diabetic foot ulcer footprints were taken a few years ago. They used three different digital cameras to take pictures of the footprints: a Nikon D300 with 24.2 megapixels, a Kodak DX530 with 5 megapixels, and a Nikon COLPIX P100 (10.3 megapixel). The images were captured by using autofocus without any zoom, macro settings, and an aperture setting of f/2.8 at approximately 30 to 40 cms from the appropriate point of the wound plane. Flashlight has not been used as the primary source of illumination; rather, only the lights within the room were allowed to be used. This was done to ensure that the finished photographs had accurate color reproduction. These photographs were taken by medical photographers who are familiar with digital field unification and have more than five years of experience in the field of physician photography. During the preliminary stage of the processing, poor-quality photographs were discarded, and released duplicates were avoided based on each file's unique hash code. Manchester Metropolitan University and the Lancashire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust provide access to digital DFU photo files that include annotations from medical practitioners [12]. The sharing of these findings is intended to motivate more scholars to conduct replicated studies in this field. There are three sorts of publicly accessible datasets that are available in academics. The first dataset consists of foot skin patches for the classification of wounds [13], the second dataset consists of regions of interest for the classification of infection and ischemia [14], and the third dataset is the most recent one made available for DFU detection.

snippet.text: The DFU mobile application was developed as an mHealth tool to provide education on diabetic foot ulcer prevention and management. The app integrates multimedia educational modules with thermal imaging capabilities to detect wound temperature, estimate wound depth and area, and support early infection risk detection. Photographs from both left and right extremities are used to quantify ulcer characteristics and provide feedback to users and caregivers. The application was built using Android Studio with Java and Kotlin programming languages and integrates a thermal imaging API compatible with FLIR sensors. A Firebase backend was used for data storage and authentication, ensuring secure and real-time access for both users and healthcare providers (Figure 1).

snippet.text:
Wounds on the feet known as Diabetic Foot Ulcers (DFUs) are a major complication of diabetes because they can become infected, leading to amputation of the foot or lower limb. In previous studies, various researchers [1][2][3][4] [5] have achieved high accuracy in the recognition of DFUs using machine learning algorithms. Additionally, researchers have demonstrated proof-of-concept in studies using mobile devices for foot image capture [6] and DFU detection [7]. However, there are still gaps in implementing these technologies across multiple devices and locations in real-world settings. To bridge these gaps, we bring world-leading researchers from international institutions to work collaboratively towards automatic DFU detection. 

The goal of the Diabetic Foot Ulcers Grand Challenge 2020 (DFUC 2020) [8] is to improve the accuracy of DFU detection in a real-world setting, and to motivate the use of more advanced machine learning techniques that are datadriven in nature. In turn, this will aid the development of a mobile app that can be used by patients, their carers, or their family members to help with remote detection and monitoring of DFU in a home setting.

snippet.text: The goal of the Diabetic Foot Ulcer Competition 2020 (DFUC 2020) dataset was to improve the accuracy of DFU detection in real-world settings (18). The dataset consisted of foot images with DFUs collected from Lancashire Teaching Hospitals. The images were captured using three digital cameras (Kodak DX4530, Nikon D3300 and Nikon COOLPIX P100), and close-ups of the foot were taken without zoom or macro functions. The dataset comprised of 4,000 images, with 2,000 used for training and 2000 for testing. The images were acquired during regular patient appointments, resulting in variability in factors such as distance, angle, lighting, and the presence of background objects. The dataset included cases with multiple DFUs, different stages of healing, partial foot visibility, and foot deformities. The dataset also featured cases with time stamps, rulers, and partial blurring or obfuscation of wounds. The images were annotated by healthcare professionals, indicating the ulcer location using bounding boxes.

Title: Diabetic Foot Ulcer Ischemia and Infection Classification Using EfficientNet Deep Learning Models
Snippet: in order to heal properly [5]. Due to the large and growing number of chronic wounds, there is an increasing demand for information technology solutions that assist the work of medical personnel, improve efficiency and reduce the cost of care. 

There are four main types of chronic wounds: pressure ulcers, diabetic foot ulcers, venous ulcers, and arterial ulcers. Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs), the focus of this paper, are a major complication of diabetes. Infection and ischemia are two common problems that occur in the healing process of DFUs, which may lead to amputation of limbs and admission of patients into hospitals [6]. After limb amputation, the patient's quality of life degrades quickly with a life expectancy of fewer than 3 years thereafter [7]. Infection occurs in 40%-80% [8] of DFUs and ischemia occurs in almost 50% of DFUs [9]. Infection is caused by the presence of bacteria in the wound, which causes cell death. DFUs are at risk of becoming infected as they are often located on the lower limbs such as on the sole of the patient's foot [10]. Ischemia is caused by insufficient blood circulation due to chronic complications of diabetes. It is essential to recognize infection and ischemia of DFUs early to reduce the risk of amputation. The economic burden of treating DFUs including infection and ischemia, ranges from $9-13 billion [11]. 

To diagnose infection and ischemia accurately, the wound bacteriology needs to be tested combined with review of patient records such as clinical history, physical health and blood tests. But this information is not always available to clinicians. Experienced wound experts are able to recognize the presence of infection and ischemia in DFUs by visual inspection. Visual cues of wound infection include increased redness in and around the ulcer, and colored purulent. Visual cues for a wound with ischemia include the presence of poor reperfusion to the foot, or black gangrenous toes (tissue death to part of the foot).

Title: Diabetic Foot Ulcers Detection Model Using a Hybrid Convolutional Neural Networks–Vision Transformers
Snippet: A significant consequence of diabetes mellitus, diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) affect millions of individuals across the globe [1]. These ulcers pose a significant public health risk, leading to morbidity, amputations, and mortality. Factors including neuropathy, ischemia, and infection delay the healing process, resulting in the formation of these ulcers [2]. DFUs have a substantial impact on individuals' quality of life [3]. Individuals with chronic wounds generally experience intense pain, restricted movement, and a lack of social interaction [4]. These wounds require extended medical consultations, dressing changes, and occasionally surgery interventions. Due to their limited physical ability and dependency on caretakers, individuals encounter depression and anxiety [5]. Hospitalization or amputations may increase the length of stay and cause substantial healthcare expenses. 

Effective DFU therapy requires timely and precise ischemia and infection identification [6]. Traditionally, DFUs diagnosis relied on laboratory testing, imaging, and clinical evaluations [7]. Clinicians identify infections using clinical symptoms, bacterial cultures, and inflammatory markers, whereas perfusion levels determine ischemia. The dependence on clinical knowledge renders these procedures laborious, subjective, and inconsistent. Imaging modalities, including thermal, hyperspectral, and fluorescence imaging have gained traction in diagnosing DFUs in the initial stages [8]. These modalities offer detailed insights into blood flow, tissue composition, and infection biomarkers [9]. However, extensive implementation costs and a steep learning curve for healthcare professionals prevent the widespread adoption of these modalities. In contrast, photographic images capture visible wound features, including size, shape, and discoloration, with sufficient clarity [10]. These features can be shared for telemedicine consultations, supporting early DFUs diagnosis. 

In the absence of prompt medical attention, ulcers have the potential to penetrate deep into soft tissue, tendons, and potentially bone, elevating the likelihood of developing osteomyelitis and systemic infections leading to the amputation of the lower extremities [10]. By using an artificial intelligence-powered DFUs detection system, healthcare personnel may initiate debridement and infection management in the early stages, preventing severe consequences [11].

Title: Deepening into the suitability of using pre-trained models of ImageNet against a lightweight convolutional neural network in medical imaging: an experimental study
Snippet: One of the complications of diabetes is diabetic foot ulcers (DFU) that can result in the removal of a foot or limb (Alzubaidi et al., 2020c). Commonly, the DFU is situated on the heel, and symptoms often include dry cracks, leg pain, foot swelling, skin temperature differences, and skin color changes. The cost of DFU treatment is usually high, and mortality rates increase if the condition is not treated at an early stage. The critical parameters for predicting the DFU's amputation risk or healing potential are detecting and diagnosing the infection or areas of ischemia (Tulloch, Zamani & Akrami, 2020). Chronic diabetes in the human body causes poor blood circulation that in turn causes ischemia (Everett & Mathioudakis, 2018). Therefore, palpating the pulses of blood flow in the foot can help discover ischemia (Amin et al., 2020), and poor foot reperfusion, which could develop into a DFU infection, shows the ischemia visually (Peter-Riesch, 2016). 

From the researchers' point of view, detecting the DFU is the objective, as (a) the appearance of DFU can change in terms of location, shape, and size, (b) resemblances between intra-and inter-class variations, and (c) lighting conditions. It should be noted that there are comprehensive, in-depth medical studies relating to leg blood vessels, blood tests, bacteriological studies, and physical examinations. However, these tests and resources are often inaccessible worldwide. This paper used a combination of two DFU datasets: (Goyal et al., 2018;Alzubaidi et al., 2020c). The first one (Goyal et al., 2018) contained 1,610 patches taken from foot images. These patches were divided into two classes: normal, with 641 patches, and abnormal, with 969 patches. The second dataset (Alzubaidi et al., 2020c) contained 1,477 patches taken from foot images, with 742 classified as normal and 735 abnormal, to provide a total of 3,087 patches.

Title: Reliability and Validation of Three Scoring Systems in the Assessment of Diabetic Foot Ulcers
Snippet: A diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) is defined as an ulceration of the foot associated with neuropathy, varying degrees of ischemia, and infection [1]. It is estimated that around 19% to 34% of patients with diabetes may develop a foot ulcer during their lifetime [2]. Diabetic foot ulcer represents one of the most serious and debilitating complications of diabetes mellitus [2]. The five-year risk of mortality for a patient with a diabetic foot ulcer is 2.5 times higher than that for a patient without a foot ulcer [2]. With such a high level of morbidity resulting from debilitating osteomyelitis and amputation in patients with DFU, it is of utmost importance to properly address and treat the underlying causes of the condition [3]. 

The sites of ulcers in diabetes are typically located in areas of the foot exposed to constant pressure or repetitive trauma [4]. Diabetic foot ulcers arise from a complex interplay of factors such as prolonged duration of diabetes, poor glycaemic control, inadequate foot care, structural foot deformities, dry skin, and repeated shear stress on the diabetic foot, leading to callus formation and subsequent ulceration [5]. These ulcers not only compromise quality of life but also significantly increase the risk of infection, hospitalization, and lower limb amputation [6]. 

Early identification of high-risk patients is therefore critical, and simple screening tools used by primary care physicians and paramedical staff can play a pivotal role in reducing morbidity and mortality [7]. Several scoring systems, including the Diabetic Ulcer Severity Score (DUSS), the Site, Ischemia, Neuropathy, Bacterial Infection, Area, and Depth (SINBAD) classification, and the University of Texas wound classification system (UT classification), have been developed to assess ulcer severity and predict outcomes [8][9][10]. Comparing these scoring systems can provide valuable insights into their relative effectiveness in forecasting wound healing in patients with DFU [11].

DFUs are at risk of becoming infected as they are often located on the lower limbs such as on the sole of the patient's foot [10]. Ischemia is caused by insufficient blood circulation due to chronic complications of diabetes. It is essential to recognize infection and ischemia of DFUs early to reduce the risk of amputation. The economic burden of treating DFUs including infection and ischemia, ranges from $9-13 billion [11]. 

To diagnose infection and ischemia accurately, the wound bacteriology needs to be tested combined with review of patient records such as clinical history, physical health and blood tests. But this information is not always available to clinicians. Experienced wound experts are able to recognize the presence of infection and ischemia in DFUs by visual inspection. Visual cues of wound infection include increased redness in and around the ulcer, and colored purulent. Visual cues for a wound with ischemia include the presence of poor reperfusion to the foot, or black gangrenous toes (tissue death to part of the foot).

documents.title: Diabetic Foot Ulcers Detection Model Using a Hybrid Convolutional Neural Networks–Vision Transformers
documents.snippet:
A significant consequence of diabetes mellitus, diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) affect millions of individuals across the globe [1]. These ulcers pose a significant public health risk, leading to morbidity, amputations, and mortality. Factors including neuropathy, ischemia, and infection delay the healing process, resulting in the formation of these ulcers [2]. DFUs have a substantial impact on individuals' quality of life [3]. Individuals with chronic wounds generally experience intense pain, restricted movement, and a lack of social interaction [4]. These wounds require extended medical consultations, dressing changes, and occasionally surgery interventions. Due to their limited physical ability and dependency on caretakers, individuals encounter depression and anxiety [5]. Hospitalization or amputations may increase the length of stay and cause substantial healthcare expenses. 

Effective DFU therapy requires timely and precise ischemia and infection identification [6]. Traditionally, DFUs diagnosis relied on laboratory testing, imaging, and clinical evaluations [7]. Clinicians identify infections using clinical symptoms, bacterial cultures, and inflammatory markers, whereas perfusion levels determine ischemia. The dependence on clinical knowledge renders these procedures laborious, subjective, and inconsistent. Imaging modalities, including thermal, hyperspectral, and fluorescence imaging have gained traction in diagnosing DFUs in the initial stages [8]. These modalities offer detailed insights into blood flow, tissue composition, and infection biomarkers [9]. However, extensive implementation costs and a steep learning curve for healthcare professionals prevent the widespread adoption of these modalities. In contrast, photographic images capture visible wound features, including size, shape, and discoloration, with sufficient clarity [10]. These features can be shared for telemedicine consultations, supporting early DFUs diagnosis. 

In the absence of prompt medical attention, ulcers have the potential to penetrate deep into soft tissue, tendons, and potentially bone, elevating the likelihood of developing osteomyelitis and systemic infections leading to the amputation of the lower extremities [10]. By using an artificial intelligence-powered DFUs detection system, healthcare personnel may initiate debridement and infection management in the early stages, preventing severe consequences [11].
