Title: Algorithms for Size and Color Detection of Smartphone Images of Chronic Wounds for Healthcare Applications
Snippet: The research group previously developed a mobile app called SmartWoundCare for Android and iOS smartphones and tablets to document and assess chronic wounds, specifically pressure ulcers (bedsores) [1]. The mobile app is part of the rapidly growing field of mobile health or mHealth, or the delivery of healthcare and healthcare support through mobile devices. Mobile consumer devices are increasingly capable of meaningful applications in mHealth, and examples range from apps that allow users to track diet and fitness, health condition monitoring (e.g. diabetes [2]; arthritis [3]), and the use of mobile devices to replace paper records and share information between healthcare providers (see [4]). 

This paper outlines the application of mobile consumer devices to automated wound analysis and classification. Specifically, work was undertaken to develop algorithms to generate wound size and to analyze wound color from a wound image taken by a smartphone or tablet camera, without the use of peripheral or auxiliary devices such as positioning templates, ultrasonic transducers, or additional lenses. This is in contrast to work by others which, for example, controls lighting and wound position with an image capture box when performing image analysis of diabetic foot ulcers [5]. The reliance on the internal smartphone sensors alone to generate high-accuracy measurements brings novelty to the work and specifically to the field of wound management.
</snippet></tool_output>

Title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Point-of-Care Fluorescence Imaging for the Detection of Bacterial Burden in Wounds: Results from the 350-Patient Fluorescence Imaging Assessment and Guidance Trial
Snippet: Objective: High bacterial load contributes to chronicity of wounds and is diagnosed based on assessment of clinical signs and symptoms (CSS) of infection, but these characteristics are poor predictors of bacterial burden. Point-of-care fluorescence imaging (FL) MolecuLight i:X can improve identification of wounds with high bacterial burden (>104 colony-forming unit [CFU]/g). FL detects bacteria, whether planktonic or in biofilm, but does not distinguish between the two. In this study, diagnostic accuracy of FL was compared to CSS during routine wound assessment. Postassessment, clinicians were surveyed to assess impact of FL on treatment plan. Approach: A prospective multicenter controlled study was conducted by 20 study clinicians from 14 outpatient advanced wound care centers across the United States. Wounds underwent assessment for CSS followed by FL. Biopsies were collected to confirm total bacterial load. Three hundred fifty patients completed the study (138 diabetic foot ulcers, 106 venous leg ulcers, 60 surgical sites, 22 pressure ulcers, and 24 others). Results: Around 287/350 wounds (82%) had bacterial loads >104 CFU/g, and CSS missed detection of 85% of these wounds. FL significantly increased detection of bacteria (>104 CFU/g) by fourfold, and this was consistent across wound types (p < 0.001). Specificity of CSS+FL remained comparably high to CSS (p = 1.0). FL information modified treatment plans (69% of wounds), influenced wound bed preparation (85%), and improved overall patient care (90%) as reported by study clinicians. Innovation: This novel noncontact, handheld FL device provides immediate, objective information on presence, location, and load of bacteria at point of care. Conclusion: Use of FL facilitates adherence to clinical guidelines recommending prompt detection and removal of bacterial burden to reduce wound infection and facilitate healing.
</snippet>

Title: Point-of-Care Autofluorescence Imaging for Real-Time Sampling and Treatment Guidance of Bioburden in Chronic Wounds: First-in-Human Results
Snippet: Background Traditionally, chronic wound infection is diagnosed by visual inspection under white light and microbiological sampling, which are subjective and suboptimal, respectively, thereby delaying diagnosis and treatment. To address this, we developed a novel handheld, fluorescence imaging device (PRODIGI) that enables non-contact, real-time, high-resolution visualization and differentiation of key pathogenic bacteria through their endogenous autofluorescence, as well as connective tissues in wounds. Methods and Findings This was a two-part Phase I, single center, non-randomized trial of chronic wound patients (male and female, ≥18 years; UHN REB #09-0015-A for part 1; UHN REB #12-5003 for part 2; clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT01378728 for part 1 and NCT01651845 for part 2). Part 1 (28 patients; 54% diabetic foot ulcers, 46% non-diabetic wounds) established the feasibility of autofluorescence imaging to accurately guide wound sampling, validated against blinded, gold standard swab-based microbiology. Part 2 (12 patients; 83.3% diabetic foot ulcers, 16.7% non-diabetic wounds) established the feasibility of autofluorescence imaging to guide wound treatment and quantitatively assess treatment response. We showed that PRODIGI can be used to guide and improve microbiological sampling and debridement of wounds in situ, enabling diagnosis, treatment guidance and response assessment in patients with chronic wounds. PRODIGI is safe, easy to use and integrates into the clinical workflow. Clinically significant bacterial burden can be detected in seconds, quantitatively tracked over days-to-months and their biodistribution mapped within the wound bed, periphery, and other remote areas. Conclusions PRODIGI represents a technological advancement in wound sampling and treatment guidance for clinical wound care at the point-of-care. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01651845; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01378728
</snippet>

Title: The Clinical Utility of Autofluorescence Imaging for Bacterial Detection in Wounds: A Systematic Review
Snippet: DaCosta et al. [37] used the PRODIGI autofluorescence (AF) device to detect bacterial presence in 28 patients with 48 wounds. 

Results were verified via swab tests. The results demonstrated that autofluorescence accurately detects bioburden in the wound bed, periphery, and off-site. AF correctly detected 74.5% of wounds with clinically significant bioburden compared with 52.5% for standard practice (p = 0.003). This was statistically significant. Additionally, AF imaging identified bacteria in the wound periphery 82.4% of the time (p < 0.001) and 67.1% in other areas (p = 0.006) which would have been overlooked using standard methods. 

In Rennie et al. [38], a total of 60 patients (45 males, 15 females) with chronic wounds, including 47 diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs), 12 venous leg ulcers (VLUs), and 1 amputation wound, were evaluated using fluorescence imaging to detect bacterial presence. Regions exhibiting red fluorescence were sampled for bacterial analysis. Of the 30 wounds sampled via biopsy in areas of red fluorescence, all tested positive for bacterial presence using quantitative PCR (qPCR) and microbiological culture, confirming a 100% positive predictive value (PPV) with no false positives. Bacterial loads ranged from 10 4 to 10 8 CFU/g, with 87% of samples exceeding ≥ 10 5 CFU/g, thresholds associated with delayed wound healing. These findings underscore the reliability of red fluorescence as a real-time, non-invasive indicator of clinically significant bacterial burden in chronic wounds. 

Ottolino-Perry et al. [9] examined the accuracy of autofluorescence (AF) imaging in identifying the bacterial burden in diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) compared to traditional clinical signs and symptoms (CSS) assessment. The study included 33 DFUs from 29 patients, with 128 swabs collected for analysis.

# Summary

Diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) infection is common and clinically critical, with guidelines emphasizing clinical assessment and prompt empiric antibiotics while recommending microbiological sampling to tailor therapy; however, accurate bacterial detection typically requires lab-quality processing, and swab-based methods are prone to contamination and miss deep-seated pathogens, leading to suboptimal pathogen yields and treatment decisions. <cite id="172f6a17-0">Infection complicates 40–80% of DFUs and major guidelines advise obtaining an appropriate specimen for culturing to guide antibiotics, yet swabs are frequently contaminated with skin flora and miss deep pathogens, prompting recommendations for tissue sampling when feasible</cite> <cite id="172f6a17-4">Diagnosis is clinical at presentation, with empiric antibiotics started promptly; swabs are quick and noninvasive, but guidelines favor tissue sampling to detect more pathogens and reduce contaminants</cite>. Real-time bacterial load estimation would be transformative, yet DFU monitoring apps predominantly focus on visual and anthropometric metrics (e.g., size, color, temperature) rather than microbiological assays, largely due to technical, regulatory, and workflow barriers, as well as the availability of specialized point-of-care devices that are not embedded into consumer apps. <cite id="f5bbec4a-0">DFU-oriented apps emphasize segmentation, size/depth, tissue classification, and telemedicine workflows, often requiring add-on hardware or structured imaging</cite> <cite id="f5bbec4a-1">Smartphone ML tools track changes over time and flag infection signs via appearance and size trends, serving as early warning systems rather than measuring microbial DNA or load</cite> <cite id="47b4053b-1">A 350-patient prospective study showed point-of-care fluorescence imaging (MolecuLight i:X) detects bacterial burden with high sensitivity relative to clinical signs and substantially increases detection of wounds with >10^4 CFU/g</cite> <cite id="47b4053b-3">Autofluorescence imaging improves detection of bioburden versus standard practice and can guide sampling and treatment in DFUs and other chronic wounds</cite>.

Below, we synthesize the reasons why real-time bacterial load estimation is not integrated into DFU apps, supported by clinical, engineering, and implementation evidence.

# 1) Clinical importance and current practice make lab-grade microbiology the norm

In DFUs, infection detection and management hinge on a clinical examination and microbiological sampling to inform antibiotics; however, sampling method and processing platform materially affect pathogen yield and appropriateness of therapy. <cite id="172f6a17-0">Swab cultures miss deep-seated pathogens and are often contaminated by skin flora, whereas tissue sampling recovers more pathogens but is invasive</cite> <cite id="172f6a17-2">Across 400 infected DFUs, tissue and swab cultures showed substantial differences: tissue reported more than one pathogen in 86.1% vs 70.1% of patients and differed in pathogen identity in 58% of patients; agreement between conventional culture and PCR was incomplete</cite>. Molecular platforms (PCR/qPCR) improve sensitivity and specificity over conventional culture, but their integration into routine DFU care relies on centralized labs and specialized workflows. <cite id="172f6a17-3">Compared with standard culture, molecular microbiology identifies more organisms from DFU samples, but it remains uncertain whether these differences change clinical decisions or outcomes</cite> <cite id="172f6a17-4">Randomized evidence indicates that tissue sampling yields more isolates and may influence prescribing, but overall clinical healing differences are small, and the practicality of point-of-care molecularization remains unsettled</cite>.

Microbial load correlates with systemic inflammation and local burden markers, reinforcing its clinical importance, yet quantification typically requires tissue biopsy and lab assays. <cite id="172f6a17-1">Total microbial load in infected DFUs positively correlates with the number of isolates on tissue cultures, white blood cell count, and platelet count, explaining 38% of variation in log microbial load</cite>. These realities set a high bar for any consumer-app–embedded “real-time bacterial load” module: it must overcome sampling contamination, achieve clinically meaningful correlation with disease activity, and match or surpass lab performance at the point of care.

# 2) Technical and engineering barriers to real-time bacterial load in smartphone apps

Smartphone DFU apps have proven effective for serial imaging, size/depth measurement, and appearance-based trend analysis, but extending them to direct bacterial load estimation faces multiple barriers: sample acquisition, assay robustness, contamination control, calibration/standardization, and device logistics.

- Sampling and contamination constraints. <cite id="172f6a17-0">Superficial swabbing is easy but contaminated with skin flora and misses deep pathogens, whereas tissue sampling better reflects infection but is invasive and logistically heavier</cite>. Embedding sterile tissue collection into a consumer app workflow, with adequate reagents and biosafety, is impractical and risky without clinical engineering safeguards. Even when using wound exudate, standard lab workflows debride and process samples to avoid confounders; replicating this onboard is beyond typical smartphone capabilities. <cite id="47b4053b-4">A field trial used wound swabs for calprotectin alongside microscopy, culture, and sensitivity, illustrating that even “point-of-care” biomarkers require careful lab handling and multiple confirmatory steps</cite>.

- Assay feasibility in the field. Existing point-of-care solutions that estimate bacterial burden rely on specialized fluorescence imaging or microfluidics, not raw smartphone photography. <cite id="47b4053b-1">MolecuLight i:X uses handheld fluorescence to detect bacterial burden with >10^4 CFU/g sensitivity fourfold higher than clinical signs, with modified treatment plans in 69% of wounds</cite>. <cite id="47b4053b-3">Autofluorescence devices detect pathogenic microflora via endogenous signals, improving detection of bioburden and guiding sampling; they were validated against blinded gold-standard microbiology</cite>. Such devices require optics, calibration, controls for excitation/emission, and validated thresholds across wound types; turning this into a “real-time CFU/mL or CFU/g” number that is clinically actionable without lab corroboration is nontrivial and not reflected in current DFU apps.

- Image and sensor variability. Even for structural/tissue metrics, phone imaging is challenged by lighting, motion, background, and camera quality, undermining reproducibility without controlled protocols. <cite id="f5bbec4a-2">Mobile wound assessment apps are limited by environmental lighting, background noise, and photo quality, making standardized capture (e.g., foot plantar imaging) necessary to make apps usable</cite>. Bacterial load estimation likely demands controlled excitation sources, dark-field/blacklight, fluorescence lifetime imaging, or microfluidic confinement—capabilities that degrade in common ambient conditions.

- Calibration and reference standards. Bacterial load reported as CFU/g or CFU/mL depends on standardized swab weights, known bacterial taxa, and validated curves; consumer devices lack on-board standards and reagent stability controls. <cite id="172f6a17-3">Molecular methods show higher organism yields than culture, and their clinical impact is uncertain; integrating these assays into uncontrolled mobile workflows raises questions about specificity and effect-size translation</cite>.

# 3) What DFU monitoring apps actually do today

Published app evaluations and examples emphasize image capture, wound size/depth measurement, color/tissue classification, and telemedicine triage—tools that support monitoring and early warning, but not pathogen detection or microbial load quantification. <cite id="f5bbec4a-0">Apps built for DFU/chronic wounds include segmentation, size/depth measurement, tissue classification, and documentation; several require add-on hardware (Structure Sensor, thermal camera, calibration markers) or specific device generations</cite> <cite id="f5bbec4a-1">DFUCare’s infection classifier achieved ~80% accuracy and flagged changes (enlargement/redness) as early warning signs of infection, while Swift Skin and Wound app provided calibrated measurements and case studies of remote infection monitoring</cite> <cite id="f5bbec4a-2">Systematic reviews catalog many wound apps (e.g., FootSnap, MOWA, thermal-camera–based ulcer detection) but note practical hurdles like lighting and image quality that necessitate structured capture</cite>. These functions are consistent with clinical practice where infection is diagnosed by examination and serial comparison, not by immediate microbial load estimation.

# 4) Clinical validation, regulatory, and workflow hurdles

Integrating bacterial load estimation into DFU apps would require multicenter prospective validation against gold standards (culture and/or qPCR), demonstrating that app-in-the-loop sampling/assay predicts clinical outcomes (e.g., healing, amputation risk, antibiotic stewardship). <cite id="172f6a17-3">Despite higher organism yields with molecular methods, it remains unknown whether sampling modality changes prescribing in clinical settings or affects clinical outcomes</cite>. Without randomized or pragmatic trials showing improved limb salvage, length of stay, or antibiotic use, payers and regulators are unlikely to support widespread deployment. Further, contamination risk and sampling inaccuracy must be proven negligible in home or primary care settings; current clinical evidence shows substantial failure to recover pathogens from swabs and frequent contamination, underscoring the need for rigorous validation before app-based deployment. <cite id="172f6a17-0">Superficial swabbing often yields contaminants and misses deep pathogens; tissue sampling is recommended but invasive and harder to standardize outside labs</cite>.

Workflow integration is another barrier. Even in specialized wound centers, adding imaging-guided sampling and rapid molecular assays requires staff training, quality assurance, and coordination with lab services; embedding this into patient-triggered app workflows adds logistics like sterile supplies, biohazard disposal, and transport of partially processed samples. <cite id="47b4053b-2">Autofluorescence imaging guided real-time sampling and debridement with 100% PPV when red fluorescence regions were biopsied and confirmed by culture and qPCR, but this was in a small first-in-human trial with specialized personnel and lab follow-up</cite>. Scaling such steps via an app implies rethinking clinic pathways and reimbursement, which are not currently in place.

# 5) Why point-of-care microbial load tools exist as specialized devices, not embedded apps

There are validated, handheld fluorescence systems that visualize and guide removal of bacteria-rich tissue, improving detection and treatment decisions; however, they operate as add-on devices and are not integrated into mainstream DFU apps, reflecting engineering, cost, and validation realities. <cite id="47b4053b-1">Point-of-care fluorescence imaging significantly outperformed clinical signs for detecting high bacterial burden and modified treatment plans in routine outpatient settings</cite> <cite id="47b4053b-3">Autofluorescence imaging detects bioburden with markedly higher accuracy than standard practice, supports mapping within wounds, and guides biopsy and debridement, validated against blinded microbiology</cite>. These platforms are specialized instruments requiring certification, calibration, and supply chains for reagents or disposables; consumer-focused apps lack the hardware, shelf-stable chemistries, and clinical-grade controls to deliver CFU/g or species-level load estimates reliably.

Moreover, clinicians already use proxies for infection (redness, swelling, warmth, purulence) and escalate to lab cultures when indicated; app-based bacterial load meters could overload workflows or be misused without robust decision support and clinician oversight. <cite id="172f6a17-4">DFU infection is diagnosed clinically at every visit with empiric antibiotics, and cultures are obtained to optimize therapy; tissue sampling increases pathogen yield but the impact on prescribing and outcomes is uncertain</cite>. In this context, apps are used to streamline triage and documentation, not replace lab microbiology.

# 6) Biomarker surrogates are emerging but not yet app-integrated

Point-of-care biomarkers in wound exudate, such as calprotectin, can help distinguish infection from noninfection, but current implementations still require careful sample handling, microscopy or immunoassays, and corroboration with culture/PCR. <cite id="47b4053b-4">A DFU study developed a wound exudate calprotectin assay alongside microscopy, culture, and sensitivity, combining markers with ulcer features to provide a diagnostic algorithm with 0.81 specificity for distinguishing mild infection from no infection</cite>. Embedding such assays into apps would entail on-device or cloud assays, reagent logistics, and clinician acceptance—steps that have not been broadly realized.

# 7) Practical constraints specific to DFUs and footwear/wound environments

Diabetic feet often have neuropathy and ischemia, altering wound exudate composition and tissue perfusion, which can affect fluorescence signal, assay kinetics, and smartphone imaging. <cite id="172f6a17-1">Microbial load correlates with systemic markers (WBC, platelets) and local ulcer features (e.g., grade), highlighting the complex interplay of host and wound factors</cite>. Thermal imaging and vision-based segmentation in DFUs face additional challenges (flat feet, similar leg morphology, hardware add-ons), limiting generalizability without strict protocols. <cite id="f5bbec4a-0">Thermal-camera–based DFU detection apps work only with attached sensors and show limited accuracy when anatomical asymmetry is absent; many visual apps require calibration markers or controlled capture</cite>. These constraints argue for lab-controlled assays over ad hoc app-based estimates.

- Robust, contamination-resistant sampling. <cite id="172f6a17-0">Adopting tissue sampling principles in minimally invasive, disposable kits that can be safely collected and stabilized for on-site assays</cite>.

- Clinical-effectiveness trials. <cite id="172f6a17-3">Demonstrate that app-guided sampling and immediate microbial load–based debridement or antimicrobial switching improves healing and reduces amputations and antibiotic overuse compared with usual care</cite>.

- Harmonized regulatory and workflow pathways. <cite id="172f6a17-4">Obtain clearance for combined hardware-software performance; define how app outputs integrate with lab results and EHRs to avoid conflicts between swab vs tissue yields and empirical therapy</cite>.

- Usability and adherence. <cite id="f5bbec4a-2">Design standardized capture workflows (positioning, lighting, background) and sensor calibration to ensure reproducibility in routine home/clinic settings</cite>.

# Conclusion

Real-time bacterial load estimation in DFU apps is clinically valuable, but current practice, technology, and logistics favor lab-grade microbiology for reliable detection and actionable results. <cite id="172f6a17-0">Sampling method and contamination critically affect pathogen yield</cite> <cite id="172f6a17-2">and swab vs tissue results often diverge substantially</cite>, while <cite id="47b4053b-1">point-of-care fluorescence imaging can significantly improve detection of high bacterial burden and guide therapy</cite> but remains a specialized device rather than a consumer app feature. <cite id="f5bbec4a-0">DFU apps are mature in size/depth/color assessment and telemedicine triage</cite> and could incorporate guided, standardized imaging for microbial-assay trigger points, but integrating validated, on-device bacterial load quantification would require breakthroughs in contamination control, assay robustness, clinical validation, and regulatory and workflow integration. Near-term solutions likely reside in pairing smartphone trend monitoring with occasional app-guided fluorescence or swab-to-lab workflows, while rigorous studies establish that real-time bacterial load estimation improves patient-centered and system outcomes. <cite id="47b4053b-4">Emerging exudate biomarkers like calprotectin improve discrimination of infection but still rely on lab processing</cite>, underscoring that app-native bacterial load estimation remains an unmet but important engineering and clinical challenge. </answer>

Title: A Comparison of Tissue versus Swab Culturing of Infected Diabetic Foot Wounds
Snippet: Diabetes patients have a 12-25% risk of developing a foot ulcer during their lifetime [1,2]. Infection is a frequent (40-80%) and costly complication of diabetic foot ulcer and represents a major cause of morbidity and mortality [3]. Consequently, causative organisms need to be reliably diagnosed and promptly controlled. 

The techniques used for sampling and microbiological analysis strongly affect the quality of evaluations of the microbiota in diabetic foot wounds. The Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends that an appropriate specimen for culturing should be obtained from diabetic foot infections (DFIs) to guide antibiotic therapy [4]. For identification of pathogens, the International Working Group on Diabetic Foot (IWGDF) has proposed that clinicians should obtain cultures from tissue specimens rather than from swabs [5,6]. Swabs are often contaminated with normal skin flora or colonizers, and their use may result in failure to identify deep tissue pathogens [7]. However, superficial wound swabbing is more widely applied in clinical practice because it is easy to perform and noninvasive. We questioned whether there is any difference in the microbiological results obtained between the two sampling techniques. A comparison of culture results from swab and tissue specimens among wounds with infections of varying severity has not yet been performed. Furthermore, the diagnostic accuracy of swab culturing in identifying different types of microorganisms has not been previously examined. 

With the aim of reappraising the reliability of superficial swabbing for the culturing of diabetic foot wounds with infections of varying severity, we prospectively compared the following two microbiological sampling techniques for the routine identification of pathogens: superficial swabbing and deep tissue biopsy. Clinical diagnosis of infection was defined by the presence of at least 2 of the following indicators: local swelling or induration, >0.5 cm of erythema around the wound, local tenderness or pain, local warmth, and purulent discharge [4,5,8].

Title: Determinants of Microbial Load in Infected Diabetic Foot Ulcers: A Pilot Study
Snippet: We examined the determinants of microbial load in infected diabetic foot ulcers in 62 patients (38 men and 24 women, mean age: 65.63 ± 12.71 years) with clinically infected diabetic foot ulcers. Tissue cultures were taken from ulcers by 4 mm punches. Ulcer grade (University of Texas classification), neuropathy disability score (NDS), neuropathy symptom score (NSS), ankle-brachial index (ABI), perfusion, extent, depth, infection, and sensation (PEDIS) grade of diabetic foot infection, and laboratory parameters were evaluated in all patients. Total microbial load was positively correlated with the number of isolates on tissue cultures (r s = 0.544, P < 0.001), white blood cell count (WBC) (r s = 0.273, P = 0.032), and platelet count (PLT) (r s = 0.306, P = 0.015). It also exhibited a borderline insignificant positive correlation with PEDIS infection grade (r s = 0.246, P = 0.053). In stepwise linear regression analysis, the number of isolates on tissue cultures and WBC were identified as the only two significant parameters accounting for 38% of the variation in the log of total microbial load (adjusted R 2 = 0.380, P < 0.001). In conclusion, patients with infected diabetic foot ulcer exhibit a positive correlation of total microbial load with the number of isolates on tissue cultures, WBC and PLT.

Title: Concordance in diabetic foot ulceration: a cross-sectional study of agreement between wound swabbing and tissue sampling in infected ulcers.
Snippet: BACKGROUND
There is inadequate evidence to advise clinicians on the relative merits of swabbing versus tissue sampling of infected diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs).


OBJECTIVES
To determine (1) concordance between culture results from wound swabs and tissue samples from the same ulcer; (2) whether or not differences in bacterial profiles from swabs and tissue samples are clinically relevant; (3) concordance between results from conventional culture versus polymerase chain reaction (PCR); and (4) prognosis for patients with an infected DFU at 12 months' follow-up.


METHODS
This was a cross-sectional, multicentre study involving patients with diabetes and a foot ulcer that was deemed to be infected by their clinician. Microbiology specimens for culture were taken contemporaneously by swab and by tissue sampling from the same wound. In a substudy, specimens were also processed by PCR. Title: Swabs versus tissue samples for infected diabetic foot ulcers: the CODIFI2 RCT.
Snippet: Background
Foot ulcers affecting people with diabetes (diabetic foot ulcers) often become infected, potentially leading to amputation. Suspected diabetic foot ulcer infection is treated with immediate empiric antimicrobials, with wound samples for culture and sensitivity collected to optimise antibiotic therapy. Collecting samples with swabs is easier than obtaining tissue, but this reports fewer pathogens and more contaminants. Compared with standard culture and sensitivity laboratory methods, molecular microbiology identifies more organisms. How these differences affect clinical decisions or outcomes is currently unknown. To determine if taking tissue samples versus swabs from suspected infected diabetic foot ulcer affects ulcer healing, antibiotic prescribing, costs of care and patient safety.


Substudy 1
To determine the agreement between microbiology results from culture and sensitivity versus molecular techniques and to assess whether intention of prescribers to change antimicrobials differs based on sampling methods.


Substudy 2
A health-economic perspective of the expected application of empiric and/or targeted treatment regimens and the cost consequences of treatment decisions based on substudy 1.


Substudy 3
To compare questionnaire response rates for theoretically informed versus standard participant letters.


Substudy 4
To explore clinician perspectives on diabetic foot ulcer sampling and processing techniques.


Design
Randomised controlled trial of results of performing tissue sampling versus swabbing of wounds in people with suspected mild or moderate infected diabetic foot ulcer. Individually randomised (allocation concealed), 1 : 1, tissue or swab sampling for suspected diabetic foot ulcer infection. Follow-up is 12-24 months. A priori sample size estimate is 730.


Substudy 1
Cross-sectional agreement study of microbiology results from molecular versus culture and sensitivity techniques and virtual clinic. Diabetic foot ulcers sampled for standard microbiology and central laboratory analysis (molecular).


Substudy 2
Exploratory cost-consequence analysis of molecular processing and the likelihood of empiric and targeted treatment based on treatment decisions from substudy 1.


Substudy 3
Randomised trial of theoretically informed versus standard participant letters.


Substudy 4
Qualitative study explored clinicians' perspectives regarding sampling and processing techniques.


Setting and participants
Twenty-one United Kingdom diabetic foot ulcer

Title: CODIFI2: Randomised controlled trial to compare clinical and cost‐effectiveness of swabs versus tissue sampling to inform management of infected diabetic foot ulcers
Snippet: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are a common complication of diabetes. 1,2 Ulcers are vulnerable to infection, with around 40% of recent-onset DFUs clinically infected at presentation. 3 Infection can lead to substantial morbidity, including amputation; hence, guidelines advise that people with a DFU should be assessed for infection at every visit. 4 he diagnosis of DFU infection is not dependent upon microbiological sampling, but requires a clinical assessment of the person, their limb, and wound. Fever, exudate, redness, inflammation, pus, odour, and bleeding indicate infection, and because the risks associated with DFU infection are substantial, empiric antibiotic therapy is initiated promptly. ][7] Clinicians often obtain ulcer specimens with a cotton swab, collecting fluid from the deep ulcer bed. 8 Swabs are readily available; sampling is quick, easy, non-invasive, and inexpensive. Clinical guidelines, however, recommend tissue sampling to detect more pathogens and reduce sampling of colonising bacteria. 4,9,10 Tissue samples identify bacteria from DFU more frequently than swabs and report more isolates per sample. 5,11,12 This could be beneficial if pathogens, rather than colonising bacteria, are found, potentially leading to more tailoring of therapeutics. Better sampling could potentially lead to more rapid resolution of infection and even quicker healing. It could also reduce the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics, reducing antibiotic resistance. 13,14 Conversely, tissue sampling's higher yield might increase prescribing. It is unknown whether using tissue sampling or swab sampling leads to changes in prescribing in clinical settings or whether any such change in prescribing affects clinical outcomes. The aim of the CODIFI2 study was to compare wound swabbing and tissue sampling in people with infected diabetic foot ulcers (DFU) to determine effects on clinical outcomes. for swab vs. tissue. The hazard ratio (HR) for healing for tissue vs. swab was 1.01 (95% CI 0.65-1.55). The median (IQR) days in hospital was 17 (12-39) for swab and 16 (10-32) for tissue.

Snippet: Apps can have one-to-many features built-in, including wound size and depth measurement, localisation and segmentation, tissue classification, manual entry of wound characteristics for documentation and monitoring, and more. Apps are typically made for assessing chronic wounds, such as PI or diabetic foot ulcers. Some apps require a portable device or component in addition to the smartphone or tablet itself. Garcia-Zapirain et al. (8) implemented a toroidal decomposition-based segmentation algorithm for PI into a tablet app that optimises the treatment plan. The same team later implemented a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based method in a tablet app to automatically segment PI wounds and measure wound size and depth (9). It is important to note that the app requires a Structure Sensor mounted on an iPad to perform the analysis. The imitoWound app (10) was developed for wound documentation and calculation of physical properties of a wound, including wound length, width, surface area, and circumference; these measurements require the use of their custom paper-based calibration markers. Fraiwan et al. (11) proposed an app that makes use of a portable thermal camera (FLIR ONE) for early detection of diabetic foot ulcers based on the Mean Temperature Difference (MTD). This smartphone app only works when attached to the external thermal imaging camera. The accuracy of the method was not benchmarked. 

Apps can be conveniently and widely used if they are designed to run on a smartphone or tablet alone. Yap et al. (12) developed an app for assessing diabetic foot ulcers called FootSnap, which the initial version captured standardised images of the plantar surface of diabetic feet and worked on iPad only. Later versions of the app (13) were trained with a CNN to localise wounds in diabetic foot ulcer images, deployed on Android platform, and proposed using a cloudbased framework to store the images taken from the app (14). Kositzke and Dujovny (15) used a wound analyser software called MOWA to perform tissue classification in Android or iOS platforms and smartphone or tablet devices.

Title: Clinical applications of machine learning for infection assessment in diabetic foot ulcers
Snippet: Machine learning is also powering smart monitoring tools that track diabetic foot ulcers over time (van Netten et al., 2017). Because infections can develop or worsen in a matter of days, continuous monitoring is crucial-especially for patients at home or in rural areas. To this end, researchers and companies have developed smartphone-based applications that use ML to analyze serial wound images. These apps enable patients or caregivers to regularly photograph their ulcers, while built-in algorithms assess healing progression and warning signs of infection. For example, DFUCare is a mobile deep-learning platform that not only detects and classifies ulcers in images, but also measures wound size and analyzes color changes on successive visits. In a pilot study, DFUCare's infection classifier achieved ∼80% accuracy and its ischemia detector ∼95% accuracy, while successfully measuring wound area within a few millimeters of error. By comparing each new image to prior ones, the system can flag if an ulcer is enlarging or if redness is increasing-potential harbingers of infection or deterioration. 

Another example is the use of the Swift Skin and Wound app (Health Canada/FDA cleared) in remote patient care (Kong et al., 2021). This app uses computer-vision to calibrate wound measurements and allows patients to upload images to their provider. A recent case report demonstrated its utility: a highrisk patient with diabetic foot ulcers used the app to send images weekly, enabling clinicians to remotely monitor three episodes of infection and adjust treatment promptly (Kong et al., 2021). The app's ML features provided objective wound size and appearance data, giving the clinician confidence in the healing trajectory and allowing intervention (e.g., starting antibiotics) at the earliest sign of recurrence. Overall, these monitoring tools leverage ML for trend analysis-they detect changes over time that might indicate an infection is not responding to treatment or that a dormant wound has become acutely infected. In resource-limited or rural settings, such smartphone apps can serve as an "early warning system, " alerting specialists to intervene before minor infections become limb-threatening.

Title: Image-Based Artificial Intelligence in Wound Assessment: A Systematic Review
Snippet: Mobile devices for wound assessment are very helpful for the convenience of use, but they can be very challenging as well because of some difficulties in environmental lighting, background noise, and photo quality. In this subsection we briefly summarize some mobile applications developed for wound assessments. Some apps are made only for wound image capturing. For example, Yap et al. [106] developed a foot imaging app called "FootSnap" using iPad to standardize image capturing of the plantar surface of diabetic feet. 

There are some mobile apps developed specifically for wound measurement and detection. A mobile wound analyzer application named MOWA, was reviewed by Manuel Dujovny in [107], which can calculate three tissue colors (black, yellow, and red), ulcer size, and wound edge dimensions. The edge of the wound requires a freehand drawing to generate the wound size. This app can also suggest therapeutic treatment advice per the international guidelines. Luay et al. [108] developed a smartphone app for ulcer detection. This app requires a mobile thermal camera (FLIR ONE) for image acquisition and based on temperature difference it can detect ulcerous areas on the feet. Though it can detect the ulcer and its location; this app does not work on a person who has one leg or if the characteristics of two legs are similar where both legs have foot complications. 

Some other smartphone apps are designed for wound healing assessments. Hettiarachchi et al. [109] developed an android mobile application for wound segmentation and to monitor the healing of chronic wounds. Wound areas are normalized for removing effects of camera distance and angle. Friesen et al. [110] developed an android app for chronic wound care that can add a new patient, store the patient information, update wound assessments, store clinical wound history, and provide a week-by-week comparison. Table IX presents a short summary of mobile applications built for wound assessments.

Title: Empowering Diabetes Patient with Mobile Health Technologies
Snippet: Diabetic foot is a main cause for nontraumatic lower limb amputation and precedes 85% of the cases. Approximately 15% of diabetes patients will develop diabetic foot ulcers in their lifetime [99]. It is recommended for all diabetes patients to perform annual extensive foot examination to identify risk factors predictive of foot ulcers. Patient should be screened for signs of peripheral neuropathy and peripheral vascular disease, simultaneously paying attention to identify other risk factors such as foot deformities, past foot ulcers, visual impairment, and cigarette smoking [97]. Currently, researched mHealth method to facilitate foot care is using high quality photography to diagnose foot ulcers and preulcerative lesions. Trained professional can diagnose visible diabetic foot changes in valid and reliable manner, which implies methods usability as a monitoring tool in home environment [100]. Originally developed was a method for wound area measurement. The wound margins are recognized with the help of smartphone. First, the wound contour is copied on the foil. The area is then measured with smartphone app and compared with previous measurements [101].

Title: Algorithms for Size and Color Detection of Smartphone Images of Chronic Wounds for Healthcare Applications
Snippet: The research group previously developed a mobile app called SmartWoundCare for Android and iOS smartphones and tablets to document and assess chronic wounds, specifically pressure ulcers (bedsores) [1]. The mobile app is part of the rapidly growing field of mobile health or mHealth, or the delivery of healthcare and healthcare support through mobile devices. Mobile consumer devices are increasingly capable of meaningful applications in mHealth, and examples range from apps that allow users to track diet and fitness, health condition monitoring (e.g. diabetes [2]; arthritis [3]), and the use of mobile devices to replace paper records and share information between healthcare providers (see [4]). 

This paper outlines the application of mobile consumer devices to automated wound analysis and classification. Specifically, work was undertaken to develop algorithms to generate wound size and to analyze wound color from a wound image taken by a smartphone or tablet camera, without the use of peripheral or auxiliary devices such as positioning templates, ultrasonic transducers, or additional lenses. This is in contrast to work by others which, for example, controls lighting and wound position with an image capture box when performing image analysis of diabetic foot ulcers [5]. The reliance on the internal smartphone sensors alone to generate high-accuracy measurements brings novelty to the work and specifically to the field of wound management.

Title: Point‐of‐care fluorescence imaging reveals extent of bacterial load in diabetic foot ulcers
Snippet: No content available

Title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Point-of-Care Fluorescence Imaging for the Detection of Bacterial Burden in Wounds: Results from the 350-Patient Fluorescence Imaging Assessment and Guidance Trial
Snippet: Objective: High bacterial load contributes to chronicity of wounds and is diagnosed based on assessment of clinical signs and symptoms (CSS) of infection, but these characteristics are poor predictors of bacterial burden. Point-of-care fluorescence imaging (FL) MolecuLight i:X can improve identification of wounds with high bacterial burden (>104 colony-forming unit [CFU]/g). FL detects bacteria, whether planktonic or in biofilm, but does not distinguish between the two. In this study, diagnostic accuracy of FL was compared to CSS during routine wound assessment. Postassessment, clinicians were surveyed to assess impact of FL on treatment plan. Approach: A prospective multicenter controlled study was conducted by 20 study clinicians from 14 outpatient advanced wound care centers across the United States. Wounds underwent assessment for CSS followed by FL. Biopsies were collected to confirm total bacterial load. Three hundred fifty patients completed the study (138 diabetic foot ulcers, 106 venous leg ulcers, 60 surgical sites, 22 pressure ulcers, and 24 others). Results: Around 287/350 wounds (82%) had bacterial loads >104 CFU/g, and CSS missed detection of 85% of these wounds. FL significantly increased detection of bacteria (>104 CFU/g) by fourfold, and this was consistent across wound types (p < 0.001). Specificity of CSS+FL remained comparably high to CSS (p = 1.0). FL information modified treatment plans (69% of wounds), influenced wound bed preparation (85%), and improved overall patient care (90%) as reported by study clinicians. Innovation: This novel noncontact, handheld FL device provides immediate, objective information on presence, location, and load of bacteria at point of care. Conclusion: Use of FL facilitates adherence to clinical guidelines recommending prompt detection and removal of bacterial burden to reduce wound infection and facilitate healing.

Title: Point-of-Care Autofluorescence Imaging for Real-Time Sampling and Treatment Guidance of Bioburden in Chronic Wounds: First-in-Human Results
Snippet: Background Traditionally, chronic wound infection is diagnosed by visual inspection under white light and microbiological sampling, which are subjective and suboptimal, respectively, thereby delaying diagnosis and treatment. To address this, we developed a novel handheld, fluorescence imaging device (PRODIGI) that enables non-contact, real-time, high-resolution visualization and differentiation of key pathogenic bacteria through their endogenous autofluorescence, as well as connective tissues in wounds. Methods and Findings This was a two-part Phase I, single center, non-randomized trial of chronic wound patients (male and female, ≥18 years; UHN REB #09-0015-A for part 1; UHN REB #12-5003 for part 2; clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT01378728 for part 1 and NCT01651845 for part 2). Part 1 (28 patients; 54% diabetic foot ulcers, 46% non-diabetic wounds) established the feasibility of autofluorescence imaging to accurately guide wound sampling, validated against blinded, gold standard swab-based microbiology. Part 2 (12 patients; 83.3% diabetic foot ulcers, 16.7% non-diabetic wounds) established the feasibility of autofluorescence imaging to guide wound treatment and quantitatively assess treatment response. We showed that PRODIGI can be used to guide and improve microbiological sampling and debridement of wounds in situ, enabling diagnosis, treatment guidance and response assessment in patients with chronic wounds. PRODIGI is safe, easy to use and integrates into the clinical workflow. Clinically significant bacterial burden can be detected in seconds, quantitatively tracked over days-to-months and their biodistribution mapped within the wound bed, periphery, and other remote areas. Conclusions PRODIGI represents a technological advancement in wound sampling and treatment guidance for clinical wound care at the point-of-care. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01651845; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01378728

Title: The Clinical Utility of Autofluorescence Imaging for Bacterial Detection in Wounds: A Systematic Review
Snippet: DaCosta et al. [37] used the PRODIGI autofluorescence (AF) device to detect bacterial presence in 28 patients with 48 wounds. 

Results were verified via swab tests. The results demonstrated that autofluorescence accurately detects bioburden in the wound bed, periphery, and off-site. AF correctly detected 74.5% of wounds with clinically significant bioburden compared with 52.5% for standard practice (p = 0.003). This was statistically significant. Additionally, AF imaging identified bacteria in the wound periphery 82.4% of the time (p < 0.001) and 67.1% in other areas (p = 0.006) which would have been overlooked using standard methods. 

In Rennie et al. [38], a total of 60 patients (45 males, 15 females) with chronic wounds, including 47 diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs), 12 venous leg ulcers (VLUs), and 1 amputation wound, were evaluated using fluorescence imaging to detect bacterial presence. Regions exhibiting red fluorescence were sampled for bacterial analysis. Of the 30 wounds sampled via biopsy in areas of red fluorescence, all tested positive for bacterial presence using quantitative PCR (qPCR) and microbiological culture, confirming a 100% positive predictive value (PPV) with no false positives. Bacterial loads ranged from 10 4 to 10 8 CFU/g, with 87% of samples exceeding ≥ 10 5 CFU/g, thresholds associated with delayed wound healing. These findings underscore the reliability of red fluorescence as a real-time, non-invasive indicator of clinically significant bacterial burden in chronic wounds. 

Ottolino-Perry et al. [9] examined the accuracy of autofluorescence (AF) imaging in identifying the bacterial burden in diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) compared to traditional clinical signs and symptoms (CSS) assessment. The study included 33 DFUs from 29 patients, with 128 swabs collected for analysis.

Title: Levels of wound calprotectin and other inflammatory biomarkers aid in deciding which patients with a diabetic foot ulcer need antibiotic therapy (INDUCE study)
Snippet: At baseline, experienced podiatrists provided a clinical assessment of participants, including an overall assessment of appearing well or unwell, checking for peri-ulcer erythema, tenderness, warmth, lymphangitis and osteomyelitis. Ankle brachial pressure indices (ABPIs) were recorded as a measure of vasculopathy, with a level less than 0.9 considered abnormal, and duplex scanning was undertaken in those with calcified vessels. Neuropathy was assessed by 10 g monofilament in the relevant foot. If the diabetic foot ulcer was judged to be infected at baseline on clinical grounds, oral antibiotics and antimicrobial dressings were prescribed based on local guidelines; oral antibiotics and antimicrobial What's new? 

• Distinguishing between mild infection and no infection in diabetic foot ulcers, a frequent position of equipoise in antibiotic prescribing, is challenging in the absence of objective evidence available at point of care. 

• We developed a novel wound exudate calprotectin assay which, when combined with venous C-reactive protein, white cell count and ulcer area, provided a diagnostic algorithm for diabetic foot ulcer infection. 

• The combined algorithm has a specificity of 0.81 in distinguishing mild infection from no infection in a diabetic foot ulcer. 

dressings were not permitted in those whose diabetic foot ulcer was judged to be uninfected. Wound swabs, without debridement, were collected for calprotectin measurement, as well as microscopy, culture and antibiotic sensitivity analysis. Venous blood was sampled for automated measurement of white cell count and CRP; serum was stored at -80 °C for analysis of procalcitonin levels. Quantification of procalcitonin was performed in duplicate by ELISA (Abcam, UK, ab100630). CRP was also measured from a pin prick of blood using a point-of-care instrument (QuikRead go CRP, Orion Diagnostica, Finland); levels were measured by a researcher and the result was not communicated to the clinician until after they had provided their overall assessment of ulcer infection status at the week 1 visit.

snippet.text: Objective: High bacterial load contributes to chronicity of wounds and is diagnosed based on assessment of clinical signs and symptoms (CSS) of infection, but these characteristics are poor predictors of bacterial burden. Point-of-care fluorescence imaging (FL) MolecuLight i:X can improve identification of wounds with high bacterial burden (>104 colony-forming unit [CFU]/g). FL detects bacteria, whether planktonic or in biofilm, but does not distinguish between the two. In this study, diagnostic accuracy of FL was compared to CSS during routine wound assessment. Postassessment, clinicians were surveyed to assess impact of FL on treatment plan. Approach: A prospective multicenter controlled study was conducted by 20 study clinicians from 14 outpatient advanced wound care centers across the United States. Wounds underwent assessment for CSS followed by FL. Biopsies were collected to confirm total bacterial load. Three hundred fifty patients completed the study (138 diabetic foot ulcers, 106 venous leg ulcers, 60 surgical sites, 22 pressure ulcers, and 24 others). Results: Around 287/350 wounds (82%) had bacterial loads >104 CFU/g, and CSS missed detection of 85% of these wounds. FL significantly increased detection of bacteria (>104 CFU/g) by fourfold, and this was consistent across wound types (p < 0.001). Specificity of CSS+FL remained comparably high to CSS (p = 1.0). FL information modified treatment plans (69% of wounds), influenced wound bed preparation (85%), and improved overall patient care (90%) as reported by study clinicians. Innovation: This novel noncontact, handheld FL device provides immediate, objective information on presence, location, and load of bacteria at point of care. Conclusion: Use of FL facilitates adherence to clinical guidelines recommending prompt detection and removal of bacterial burden to reduce wound infection and facilitate healing.

snippet.text: Background Traditionally, chronic wound infection is diagnosed by visual inspection under white light and microbiological sampling, which are subjective and suboptimal, respectively, thereby delaying diagnosis and treatment. To address this, we developed a novel handheld, fluorescence imaging device (PRODIGI) that enables non-contact, real-time, high-resolution visualization and differentiation of key pathogenic bacteria through their endogenous autofluorescence, as well as connective tissues in wounds. Methods and Findings This was a two-part Phase I, single center, non-randomized trial of chronic wound patients (male and female, ≥18 years; UHN REB #09-0015-A for part 1; UHN REB #12-5003 for part 2; clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT01378728 for part 1 and NCT01651845 for part 2). Part 1 (28 patients; 54% diabetic foot ulcers, 46% non-diabetic wounds) established the feasibility of autofluorescence imaging to accurately guide wound sampling, validated against blinded, gold standard swab-based microbiology. Part 2 (12 patients; 83.3% diabetic foot ulcers, 16.7% non-diabetic wounds) established the feasibility of autofluorescence imaging to guide wound treatment and quantitatively assess treatment response. We showed that PRODIGI can be used to guide and improve microbiological sampling and debridement of wounds in situ, enabling diagnosis, treatment guidance and response assessment in patients with chronic wounds. PRODIGI is safe, easy to use and integrates into the clinical workflow. Clinically significant bacterial burden can be detected in seconds, quantitatively tracked over days-to-months and their biodistribution mapped within the wound bed, periphery, and other remote areas. Conclusions PRODIGI represents a technological advancement in wound sampling and treatment guidance for clinical wound care at the point-of-care. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01651845; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01378728

snippet.text:
DaCosta et al. [37] used the PRODIGI autofluorescence (AF) device to detect bacterial presence in 28 patients with 48 wounds. 

Results were verified via swab tests. The results demonstrated that autofluorescence accurately detects bioburden in the wound bed, periphery, and off-site. AF correctly detected 74.5% of wounds with clinically significant bioburden compared with 52.5% for standard practice (p = 0.003). This was statistically significant. Additionally, AF imaging identified bacteria in the wound periphery 82.4% of the time (p < 0.001) and 67.1% in other areas (p = 0.006) which would have been overlooked using standard methods. 

In Rennie et al. [38], a total of 60 patients (45 males, 15 females) with chronic wounds, including 47 diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs), 12 venous leg ulcers (VLUs), and 1 amputation wound, were evaluated using fluorescence imaging to detect bacterial presence. Regions exhibiting red fluorescence were sampled for bacterial analysis. Of the 30 wounds sampled via biopsy in areas of red fluorescence, all tested positive for bacterial presence using quantitative PCR (qPCR) and microbiological culture, confirming a 100% positive predictive value (PPV) with no false positives. Bacterial loads ranged from 10 4 to 10 8 CFU/g, with 87% of samples exceeding ≥ 10 5 CFU/g, thresholds associated with delayed wound healing. These findings underscore the reliability of red fluorescence as a real-time, non-invasive indicator of clinically significant bacterial burden in chronic wounds. 

Ottolino-Perry et al. [9] examined the accuracy of autofluorescence (AF) imaging in identifying the bacterial burden in diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) compared to traditional clinical signs and symptoms (CSS) assessment. The study included 33 DFUs from 29 patients, with 128 swabs collected for analysis.

At baseline, experienced podiatrists provided a clinical assessment of participants, including an overall assessment of appearing well or unwell, checking for peri-ulcer erythema, tenderness, warmth, lymphangitis and osteomyelitis. Ankle brachial pressure indices (ABPIs) were recorded as a measure of vasculopathy, with a level less than 0.9 considered abnormal, and duplex scanning was undertaken in those with calcified vessels. Neuropathy was assessed by 10 g monofilament in the relevant foot. If the diabetic foot ulcer was judged to be infected at baseline on clinical grounds, oral antibiotics and antimicrobial dressings were prescribed based on local guidelines; oral antibiotics and antimicrobial What's new? 

• Distinguishing between mild infection and no infection in diabetic foot ulcers, a frequent position of equipoise in antibiotic prescribing, is challenging in the absence of objective evidence available at point of care. 

• We developed a novel wound exudate calprotectin assay which, when combined with venous C-reactive protein, white cell count and ulcer area, provided a diagnostic algorithm for diabetic foot ulcer infection. 

• The combined algorithm has a specificity of 0.81 in distinguishing mild infection from no infection in a diabetic foot ulcer. 

dressings were not permitted in those whose diabetic foot ulcer was judged to be uninfected. Wound swabs, without debridement, were collected for calprotectin measurement, as well as microscopy, culture and antibiotic sensitivity analysis. Venous blood was sampled for automated measurement of white cell count and CRP; serum was stored at -80 °C for analysis of procalcitonin levels. Quantification of procalcitonin was performed in duplicate by ELISA (Abcam, UK, ab100630). CRP was also measured from a pin prick of blood using a point-of-care instrument (QuikRead go CRP, Orion Diagnostica, Finland); levels were measured by a researcher and the result was not communicated to the clinician until after they had provided their overall assessment of ulcer infection status at the week 1 visit.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer FAILS part (1) of the criterion. It does NOT confirm through cited app literature that current DFU monitoring apps do NOT provide real-time bacterial load estimation. Instead, the answer describes what apps DO measure (size, depth, color, tissue classification, telemedicine workflows) in references [3], [4], and [11], but never cites a systematic review, app inventory study, or explicit statement from app literature that confirms the ABSENCE of bacterial load capability. References [3], [4], and [11] describe app features but do not explicitly state that bacterial load estimation is missing from all surveyed apps. The answer's statement 'DFU monitoring apps predominantly focus on visual and anthropometric metrics... rather than microbiological assays' is a synthesis/inference by the author, not a direct confirmation from cited literature. Part (2) is partially satisfied—the answer provides multiple evidence-grounded barriers (sampling contamination [1], assay feasibility requiring specialized fluorescence devices [5][6], image variability [11], clinical validation requirements [8], workflow integration challenges), but these barriers are undermined by the failure to first establish definitively that apps lack this feature.
other_issues: The answer is extremely verbose and repetitive (e.g., sampling contamination issues are discussed in sections 1, 2, 4, and 7; fluorescence imaging capabilities are repeated in sections 2, 5, and 8), making it difficult to extract the core argument.

Section headings promise to explain 'why' barriers exist but often just restate what the barriers are without causal mechanism (e.g., section 4 lists validation/regulatory hurdles but doesn't cite specific regulatory frameworks or device classification requirements).

The answer conflates two distinct technologies: (a) consumer smartphone apps for wound monitoring, and (b) specialized handheld fluorescence devices (MolecuLight i:X, PRODIGI). It acknowledges these are separate but doesn't cite literature explaining WHY the fluorescence technology cannot be integrated into smartphone apps (e.g., hardware constraints, cost, FDA clearance pathways).

References [5], [6], [12] describe handheld fluorescence devices that DO provide bacterial burden detection, but the answer does not cite technical literature explaining the specific hardware (excitation wavelengths, optical filters, calibration requirements) or regulatory (510(k) vs. mobile medical app guidance) barriers preventing smartphone integration.

The answer does not cite regulatory frameworks explicitly—no reference to FDA mobile medical app guidance, EU MDR device classification, or clinical trial requirements for diagnostic claims, despite claiming these are barriers.
Minor: The summary section at the top is redundant with the rest of the answer and adds little value.
judgment.summary: The answer provides extensive discussion of technical, clinical, and workflow barriers to bacterial load estimation in DFU apps, grounded in multiple citations. However, it FAILS the verification criterion because it does not cite app literature explicitly confirming that current apps lack bacterial load capability—it only describes what apps do measure and infers the absence. The answer would pass if it cited a systematic review or app inventory stating 'none of the 20 reviewed DFU apps provide bacterial load estimation' or similar. Additionally, while barriers are discussed at length, the answer lacks citations for specific regulatory pathways or technical hardware constraints that would make smartphone integration infeasible.
